stalest flag**, and **a question somebody else wrote down**. Both produced a bug.

### The dogfood: `--dithered --editor`, the stalest flag (last run 2026-10-11)

Mechanically healthy, and read as one paragraph rather than for errors:

* **The dithered canvas is where it was recorded** — `1212×784` from 78 subs, coverage `0..40`, one panel 11,
  all four matching the sample's stamped shape. Auto's trim **30.6 %** against the recorded 30.3 % apron
  (the window is 25–36 %; the 15 % bar is for a *tiled* canvas, and this shape's apron is genuinely wide).
  The panel map and the per-panel grain note are silent, which this sample's own `[NB]` explains and a test
  pins: its 0.667° frame steps panels 0.547° against a 0.25° `PANEL_LINK_DIST_DEG`, so the re-frame that makes
  the depths a continuum also chains one panel to the next. `--mosaic` is the control and does draw the map.
* **Page heights at the standing DOGFOOD BASELINE**: `/life-list [Still to shoot]` **14,513 px** on a phone
  against the recorded 14,513/14,492; the dithered Target page 3,850 px. Nothing overflowing, no console
  errors, both editor drives re-rendering all 21 ops with Undo/Redo live.
* **The three Target cards agree.** `🎯 Nicely framed` on the mosaic against `🧩 It's bigger than one frame`
  on the single field is the pair behaving correctly, and next-best-move, the readiness card and the grain
  measurement all price the depth **per panel** ("your 13 min is spread across about 6 fields of sky, so a
  typical part of this picture has 2 min so far").
* **The known near-finding was re-checked against the record, not re-filed**: `next-best-move` and
  `framing-verdict` saying nearly the same thing on the single field is v0.443.0 working as designed (recorded
  2026-10-14 below). The "Star cluster" verdict on M 42 is the filed ⚪ `classify_target` confidence entry.

**The one finding, and it is real.** On the dithered run the probe tapped the live chip "Too dark" and
reported *"the taste 'Too dark' just taught has no note — and the Reset link lives inside it, so there is now
no way to undo it"*, then *"no Reset link to undo the two taps — the scratch library keeps them"* (its own
cleanup failed for the same reason). The field-sample drive, three minutes earlier in the same pass, had shown
the note. **v0.495.15** below is that bug.

### v0.495.15 — the tap that creates a taste took away the only way to undo it

`AutoFeedback`'s module docstring promises the taste is *"fully reversible"*, with *"a one-tap Reset back to
the neutral, data-driven default"*. The Reset link is rendered **inside** the "why Auto shifted" line
(`{note ? <Text>{note} <Anchor>Reset</Anchor></Text> : null}`), and `mergeMeasuredPreferences` deliberately
keeps *the last measured note* across a scoped tap rather than the server's un-narrowed one —
`note: scoped && !data.neutral ? (old?.note ?? null) : data.note` — because the POST measures no picture and
its sentence can claim something about *this* image that is not true.

That reasoning is right, and **the first tap is the one case where "keep the last measured note" has nothing
to keep.** A neutral profile has no note, so `old?.note` is `undefined`, so `note` becomes `null` — and the
control went with the sentence, immediately after the tap that created the taste, until the background
re-read landed. On the owner's mosaic that re-read sits behind the Auto re-run the same tap starts
(`if (!limit) onRerun()`), which this repo measures in seconds at his scale; on the 6-frame field sample it is
a blink, which is why five editor drives never saw it and the first `--dithered --editor` pass did.

**The sharpest part is that the engine had already written the invariant down.**
`seestack/edit/auto_prefs.describe_profile`'s docstring: *"**Nothing is dropped** … the note is the only place
the Reset link lives, so a note that vanished would take a control with it."* The engine keeps it exactly —
`describe_profile` returns `None` on precisely the condition `is_neutral` is true, so a non-neutral profile
always comes with a sentence. **The client was manufacturing the one state the server is careful never to
serve.** Same class as v0.495.11/.12 (a stale consumer of a fact that gained a second author) read from the
other end: here the *consumer* synthesised an impossible value, and the owner of the invariant was a docstring
in another language.

The fix separates the control from the sentence: `resettable = !prefs.data.neutral` — the server's own answer
to "is there a taste to undo?", which the POST carries for free — and the line renders on `note || resettable`,
with a new `AUTO_TASTE_PLAIN_NOTE` ("Auto has learned a taste from your taps.") standing in while the measured
sentence is in flight. That stand-in claims only what `neutral: false` establishes and **nothing about this
picture**, which is the line the narrowing draws; borrowing the un-narrowed note to fill the gap would have
undone v0.492.56/.57. Nothing moves in the decided cases: a neutral profile still offers no Reset (two
existing tests), and a tap that walks the last bias back to neutral still drops both (a third).

Tests +1, red before, measured by reverting the two render lines alone: **exactly** that test fails and the
other 31 in the file pass. The suite's own shape shows why it was never asked — the pending-refetch test
starts from a profile that *already has* a note, and the neutral-start test lets the refetch resolve
immediately.

### v0.495.14 — a merged spec is a question list, and answering one found the solve path with no test behind it

`docs/design/settings-redesign.md` shipped with a question addressed to whoever builds slice 1: *"confirm how
the solver uses `astap_fov_deg` vs the frame's own `FOCALLEN`/`XPIXSZ` before wiring 'Read from my photos'"*.
Answering it is not slice 1 and collides with nothing. The answer, traced through every consumer:

- `solve/runner.py::solve_one` derives the FOV from the frame (`_fov_deg_for_frame` →
  `fits_loader.fov_deg_from_header`) and uses the passed value only when the header cannot answer;
- `solve/bootstrap.py` — the rescue path — does the same for the deep image it builds, off the **reference
  sub's** header (`_fov_deg_for_frame(paths[ref_index], fov_deg)`);
- **nothing uses the setting unconditionally.** Settings' own "Test ASTAP" button looked like the exception and
  is not: `routers/system.py` solves a *real ingested frame* through `solve_one`, so it re-derives too.

So the warning the spec proposed — *"If this doesn't match the telescope that took the photos, most frames
won't be placed"* — is **false of any Seestar frame**, and it would have been the scariest sentence in the
table on the page whose whole purpose is to stop settings being scary; the spec's own rule ("Every warning must
be true of the code") decides it. Two more consequences are now written into that row: "Read from my photos"
cannot be one of three *choices*, because reading from the photos is unconditional and cannot be switched off;
and a three-way control cannot be stored at all, since `astap_fov_deg` is
`float = Field(default=1.3, ge=0.1, le=20.0)` and an "auto" value would re-type the field, which the spec's own
"UI only" rule and §9 both forbid.

**And the read found the gap.** `solve_one`'s derivation is pinned both ways. The bootstrap path reaches ASTAP
by its own route — it writes a temp deep image carrying no optics headers and hands `_default_deep_solver` the
FOV explicitly — and **27 tests over `tests/test_bootstrap_solve.py` asserted nothing about that number**
(`grep -n fov` on the file: no hits). Passing `fov_deg` straight through would have left all 27 green while
sending an S30's 2.1° field as the 1.3° fallback, on exactly the subs that already failed to solve once —
the historical failure AGENTS.md §1 names on the owner's own hardware.

**The fixture is the whole test.** `_make_project_with_faint_subs` writes **no** `FOCALLEN`/`XPIXSZ`, which is
the one state in which the fallback *is* right, so a test built on it would have passed for the wrong reason —
§8's "a regression test whose fixture cannot show the bug is green for the same reason".
`_make_project_with_faint_s30_subs` adds the owner's own optics (150 mm, 2.9 µm), where the derived field is
0.2659° against a deliberately absurd 7.5° fallback, and the test asserts **all** members derive one number so
it cannot pass by landing on a different reference sub. Fail-before measured in a scratch worktree:
`ref_fov = _fov_deg_for_frame(…)` → `ref_fov = fov_deg` gives `assert 7.5 == 0.2658526666666667`, with the
no-optics control still green. No production line changed in that version — the code was already right; what
was missing was anything that would notice if it stopped being.

### Four reads that did NOT become findings, recorded so they are not redone

- **`webapp/edit_resume_cache`'s boundary against `edit_fit_cache`'s fingerprints.** `boundary()` returns a
  position in the **enabled** op list while `remember()` stores `op_fingerprints(recipe)`, so a disabled op
  inside the prefix looked like it would misalign the comparison — disabling a background op would then keep
  its effect *and* skip the user's own stretch. It cannot: `op_fingerprints` already filters disabled ops, so
  the two are the same list. The shape is exactly that of a real bug; the answer is one docstring away.
- **The Settings form clobbering unsaved edits.** `SettingsView` seeds its form from an effect
  (`if (settings.data) setForm(settings.data)`), so any refetch mid-edit would wipe the owner's work silently.
  Closed by `frontend/src/queryDefaults.ts` — `refetchOnWindowFocus: false` — plus TanStack's structural
  sharing keeping `data` identity when the payload is deep-equal. **Worth knowing now rather than later:**
  slice 1 rewrites that file, and any slice that adds a query to the page or touches its staleTime re-opens it.
- **Clearing a number field is silently a no-op.** `dropEmptyFields` drops `""` from the save patch, so a
  cleared box keeps its stored value while the toast still says "Settings saved". Deliberate and tested
  (`Settings.test.tsx`: the alternative was a 422 that discarded every other edit in the form). The
  consequence for slice 1 is that **"Back to default" has to be an explicit control, never a cleared box.**
- **A pointer from the Library wall to the #903 repair — declined, once, so it is not re-litigated.** The wall
  chips each flat picture but the one-click library-wide repair lives only in Settings → Maintenance, so 44
  flat targets read as 44 clicks. `webapp/routers/unstretched.py`'s own docstring already decided this: *"It
  names; it never acts … there is no 'fix them all' button"*, with the #903 repair as the single narrow,
  owner-requested exception — and the owner asked for that repair himself on 2026-09-26, so he knows where it
  is. A second always-on line on the wall would be new surface against his standing clutter complaint, buying
  a click he has already been told about.

### The method note: the cheapest work available to a blocked run is somebody else's written-down question

A spec, a stand-down, a "confirm X before building Y" — each is a read of the code that somebody already
decided was necessary, and answering one costs minutes and collides with nothing. This run's answer was going
to be three sentences in a table cell; on the way to it every consumer of one setting got read, which is how
the untested rescue path turned up. The same shape twice over: the dogfood flag nobody had run in three days
found the editor bug.

**And my own first draft of that table cell was wrong, in the way this file keeps criticising.** I wrote "the
self-test has no frame to read" off a `grep` line instead of opening the function — `routers/system.py` solves
a real ingested frame. The guard is the one already written here: re-derive the premise, **including your
own**, and prefer reading the function to reading its call site.

### One cost of shipping two versions in one PR, measured after the fact

This PR carried **v0.495.14 and v0.495.15** as two independently-green commits, because the harness pins a run
to one branch and §5's "any one can be reverted alone" is about the commits rather than the merges. After the
merge, `git tag --list` shows **v0.495.15 and no v0.495.14**: `release-tags.yml` tags "every version
transition on main's **first-parent line**", and an intermediate version only ever existed on the branch side
of the merge, so it is never a transition there.

**It is not a reuse hazard, which was the thing worth checking.** `scripts/check-version-bump.sh`'s first arm
refuses any `__version__` that is not strictly newer than the one on `main`, so with `main` at 0.495.15 no
later PR can ship 0.495.14 — the tag arm never has to catch it. What *is* lost is one line of the tagger's own
promise ("a deploy or a rollback can name an exact build, `git checkout v0.455.7`"): there is no
`v0.495.14` to check out, only the merge above it and the branch commit below.

So the rule, for a run deciding between one PR and two: **one version per merge if the intermediate state is
worth being able to check out by name; two in one PR is fine when it is not.** Neither is wrong — §8's "one
change per merge" is about revertability, which the separate commits already give — but the tag only ever
lands on the last one.

### The §8 trailer drift — recorded, deliberately not guarded

Of the last 300 commits' `Co-Authored-By:` trailers, **66 read `Claude Opus 5`, 5 `Claude Opus 4.8`, 3
`Claude Opus 5.5` and 15 `Claude`** — the majority carry a model identifier, which §8 forbids outright ("never
put a model identifier in commits, code or logs") and which the recorded resolution of this disagreement
(2026-10-11, below) settles as `Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>` and nothing else. This run's
commits use that form.

`scripts/check-commit-identity.sh` does not catch it and **was deliberately left alone**: it is an *email*
guard, and extending it to refuse a model identifier would start refusing other runs' pushes over a point
their kickoff prompts actively ask for. A guard that makes concurrent runs fight their own instructions is not
a Builder's call — it is "needs owner sign-off" at most. Filed here, as §0 directs, rather than built.

## 2026-10-14 (Builder, branch `claude/determined-pasteur-7wyfto`) — a "flake" whose premise was wrong by 20×, and what that says about flakes in general

*(→ **v0.495.13**. Baseline: `main`'s CI run **2307** still in flight on the exact HEAD `06c255da`
(v0.495.12), with **four of five jobs already green** — Frontend build + tests, Image contract, Version bump
is sane, Commit identity — and run **2305** green before it; the local suite agreed. Inbox **four open**,
confirmed with `list_issues`: #878, #880, #903, #1015, all previously acted-on and owner-gated. **No open
PRs**, so §11's claim check was a formality.)*

### Reading the *jobs* of an in-flight run is most of a baseline

The previous two runs' note — read `main`'s own CI result before spending seventy minutes on a local
suite — has a cheap extension: a run that is still `in_progress` is not a blank. `list_workflow_jobs`
on it showed Frontend, Image contract, Version and Identity all green with only Python tests outstanding,
which is enough to know `main` is not red in any way this run's change could collide with. One call,
seconds, on a run that would not report for another half-hour.

### The finding: the entry with an actionable shape was a misfiled real bug

Of the top four "Bugs" entries, three are decided stand-downs or gated on a number only the owner's library
has. The fourth was the `Editor.test.tsx` *"Unable to find an element with the text: Stretch"* failure, filed
the same morning as a `findByText` timeout flake with two proposed shapes, of which (a) was *"give this file
an explicit `asyncUtilTimeout` — testing-library's default is 1 s"*.

**`frontend/src/test/setup.ts` has configured `asyncUtilTimeout: 20000` since the previous round of this**,
under twenty lines of comment recording the 5 000 ms and 10 000 ms attempts that preceded it. So the wait had
not expired at 1 s; it had waited **twenty seconds** for ops that were never coming back. And
`Editor.test.tsx:1671`, the line the job log names, is not one of the three static-toolbar waits the entry
describes — it is two lines after the `fireEvent.click` inside *"offers the user's saved default recipe"*.

Both facts were inside the artefacts the entry itself linked, one command each. The entry was filed carefully
and in good faith: it named its confidence, refused to flip a constant blind, and ended *"do not simply
re-run and move on"* — which is the sentence that produced the fix. The gap is narrower and more ordinary
than carelessness: **a filing is written by the run that could not finish the work, so its premise is a
hypothesis with a citation, not a measured fact.** Re-derive the premise before building on it — and in this
case the re-derivation (`cat setup.ts`, read the line number) was cheaper than the fix.

### The general lesson: "only under load" and "a real bug" are not alternatives

The reason the flake framing is seductive is that it explains the pattern perfectly — green locally, red on a
loaded runner, red on a diff that cannot have caused it. But **contention does not invent failures; it
changes which order two async settles land in**, and that is precisely what a race needs in order to become
visible. The editor's first-open decision waits for *both* of its seed reads while each nudge button renders
on *its own*, so whichever read is slower sets the width of a window in which the pipeline is interactive but
undecided — and `vi.fn().mockResolvedValue()` on two queries is not a fixed order.

So the test for a "wait longer" fix is one question: **what is this wait waiting for, and is anything still
going to deliver it?** Here nothing was: `openOn([])` had already reset the pipeline the click filled. A
raised timeout would have turned a reproducible red into an intermittent one and buried a user-facing bug
under a constant.

### What the fix is careful about, for whoever touches it next

- **`adoptWhatTheUserBuilt` must not reset the undo history.** The notification that puts a seed in the
  pipeline promises *"Undo to revert"*, so adopting the work with `openOn` (which clears history) would trade
  one silent loss for another. It writes only the two keys.
- **Its keys are `openOn`'s**, taken from the saved recipe — which is empty in the only state it is reachable
  in — so the decided case (every open where both reads land before a click) is byte-identical to before, and
  the leave guard still reads the click as unsaved work.
- **`pipelineWritten` is cleared on a run change, not by the reset it guards.** The outgoing run's edits are
  not a write to the incoming run's pipeline, and the hand-over reset deliberately happens a beat *later*
  (it is what keeps the previous run's recipe on screen instead of flashing empty).
- **Every `setOps` caller was checked to be a user action** before the flag was given that meaning: every
  one is an event handler or a mutation callback, and none is in an effect — which is what lets
  "something wrote the pipeline" stand in for "the user wrote the pipeline".

### Measuring a frontend fail-before without touching the running suite

The Python suite was running for the whole investigation, and §7 forbids editing the tree under it —
`git stash` included. `git worktree add <scratch> origin/main` plus a symlink to the real
`frontend/node_modules` gave a complete, independent frontend to write the fix and the tests in, at the cost
of one `ln -s`. The 2026-10-05 caveat (a worktree does not isolate a module your change *adds*) does not
apply here: the change edits an existing file, which resolves from the worktree. Fail-before was taken by
`git checkout -- frontend/src/routes/Editor.tsx` inside the worktree — 4 red — and the file restored from a
copy — 4 green.

## 2026-10-14 (Builder, branch `claude/relaxed-cray-4uwet8`) — the backlog was dry, so the run asked "who else reads this?" and the dogfood pass was clean

*(→ **v0.495.11** + **v0.495.12**. Baseline: `main`'s own CI run **2300** green on the exact HEAD
`9e19088d` (v0.495.10) — read first, per the previous run's note, and the local suite then agreed at
**7941 passed, 7 skipped** in 21m28s. Inbox **four open**, confirmed with `list_issues`: #878, #880, #903,
#1015, every one previously acted-on and owner-gated, nothing new owed. PR **#1161** was live (its branch
pushed 33 minutes before this run began) and had filed the top two "Bugs" entries within the previous ~1.5 h,
so §11 made both claimed-in-spirit and this run took neither; #1161 merged mid-run and this branch took the
union.)*

### Two gates closed by reading, which is what turned a dry backlog into two fixes

"Bugs" really did hold nothing ungated, and that was established rather than inherited from
[`FOCUS.md`](FOCUS.md). Two entries were read down to their source before being left alone: the **"full data"
TIFF white point**, whose archived 2026-09-03 trace gates it on his own pixels (`(p99.99 − p1) / (max − min)`
on a real deep OSC stack), and **observer #903's residual**, where the useful discovery is that the repair
*shipped* — v0.479.3's "Give back pictures a restack flattened" — so what is left really is his click.
"Features that serve real workflows" was read end to end: every entry shipped, closed, or deliberately
declined.

**Reading v0.479.3 adversarially is what found the work**, and the reason to read it was arithmetic rather
than suspicion: 44 of his pictures depend on that one function, and it had never been looked at since the
module underneath it changed. Both bugs this run shipped are in code that was *correct when written*.

### The method: when a module gives an old fact a new author, grep the readers

v0.492.13 added provenance to a target's cover — `seestack/coverpin.py`, `app_pin_reason`, a careful module
docstring — and converted the three call sites it was about (`io/library.py` writes,
`pipeline._displayed_picture_state` and `routers/newsubs.py` read). It did the hard part right. Both of this
run's bugs are sites it was **not** about, and both came out of one mechanical pass: `grep -rn
'cover_stack_run_id'` over `seestack/` and `webapp/`, then of each hit ask only *"does this ask **which**
picture, or does it ask **who chose** it?"*

That question does the whole separation. A dozen hits are pass-throughs to `displayed_picture_run` /
`_representative_run` / `current_picture_path` — "which run is displayed" is correct **whoever** pinned it, so
none of them is a bug and none needed touching. Exactly four carry an authorship *claim*, and two of them had
never been converted:

- **`refinish.py` (v0.495.11)** stood down on "a cover is set" and reported `cover_pinned` — *"somebody chose
  the picture"* — for a pin the app had placed. Only `PIN_REASON_MERGE` can reach it, and that is **asserted
  in both directions** rather than reasoned about: `merge_targets_result` pins whatever the destination was
  *showing* (`_displayed_run_id` deliberately never asks whether it is finished), while
  `PIN_REASON_KEPT_FINISHED` sits on a finished picture and so has already returned `None` two lines earlier.
- **`gallery.py::get_best_pictures` (v0.495.12)** fed the same "a cover is set" bool to `rank_portfolio`,
  which sorts on `not entry.pinned` **first** — so a Combine's own pin outranked *every* unpinned picture on
  "My best pictures" and could push his genuinely best ones off `limit`.

Both are one condition. Neither moves a cover, a pin or a precedence, and in both the pinned run stays the
target's **representative**, because that part was never wrong.

### The sharper half: the app had already written the correct sentence somewhere else

`frontend/src/components/mergeSuggestions.ts::mergeCoverClause` exists to tell the user about this very pin,
and its comment calls it *"a cover the user never pinned"* — in the confirmation he reads. Two Python modules
away, the same pin was his favourite and his choice. **A contradiction between something the app *says* and
something the app *does* is cheap to grep for and is where this class lives**; it is a better starting point
than re-reading the module that looks suspicious, because the correct wording is already in the tree and
somebody has already thought it through.

### Dogfood: `--calibration --incoming-lag` — CLEAN, and the one thing that looked like a finding was a fix working

Run in the CI wait, on the two stalest flags (§7 forbids it beside `pytest`, so it went between the suites).
**0 findings, nothing overflowing, no console errors**, every page height on the standing baseline. The
calibration branch was genuinely exercised rather than merely reached: two masters built and in the registry,
the defect scan reporting 31 hot/dead pixels (0.020 %), `auto_bind_calibration` on, the stack **actually
calibrated** (`masters actually applied: {'dark_master_id': 1, 'flat_master_id': 2}`), both binds `confident`,
the stack-health card saying *"calibrated (dark+flat)"* — and the `health/calibration` note correctly
**silent**, which the log makes you disambiguate by reading the `[run]` line: silent because the masters were
applied (the right reason), not because nothing was.

**The near-finding is worth recording so the next run does not file it.** Reading the Target page's paragraph
as one block, two *inline* cards say nearly the same thing: `next-best-move` (*"only about 20% of it made it
in … Shooting it in mosaic mode next session is the biggest win"*) and `framing-verdict` (*"It's bigger than
one frame … only about 20% … Shoot it in mosaic mode"*). That reads as duplication on the page the owner
called "extremely busy" — but it is **v0.443.0 working as designed**: `nextBestMove` claims to name *the
single* highest-leverage move and had never heard of framing, so that fix added a `framing` rung precisely so
the two would stop prescribing **different** next sessions. Agreement between a card that *ranks* and a card
that *explains* is the intended outcome; it looks like repetition and is not a bug. The probe's own preamble
says four of the last five findings were two of these cards disagreeing — the inverse case needs the same
check before it is filed.

### One environment trap, paid for in this run

Narrowing a fix with an ad-hoc file list, `tests/webapp/test_gallery_best.py tests/test_portfolio.py
tests/webapp/test_refinish.py` came back **`E fixture 'built_library' not found`** on the whole last file —
which reads exactly like a broken checkout or a bad conftest. It is neither: **naming test files from two
directories in one invocation can make a later `tests/webapp/` file lose `tests/webapp/conftest.py`'s
fixtures.** Measured with order as the only variable: `tests/test_portfolio.py tests/webapp/test_refinish.py`
→ 38 passed; `tests/webapp/test_unstretched.py tests/test_portfolio.py tests/webapp/test_refinish.py` → 47
passed **and 16 errors**, all in the last file while the first webapp file was fine. The same files pass alone
and in the full suite. Confirmed pre-existing by re-running the identical list on a clean tree. Written up in
[`AGENT-ENVIRONMENT.md`](AGENT-ENVIRONMENT.md); the habit is **one directory per invocation**, and the tell is
an *error at setup* naming a fixture that plainly exists.

### §11, and the cost of the "one version per PR" rule

Two fixes meant two PRs, because the previous collision note is explicit that a PR carrying two versions gets
only its head one tagged. With the harness pinning this run to a single branch name, that meant shipping them
strictly in series: sync, full suite, merge, then re-sync the second onto the new `main` and run the full
suite again — **four 21-minute suites for two one-line fixes**. The CI wait is where the dogfood pass and
these notes were written, which is the only reason the cost was tolerable. Worth knowing before choosing to
batch: a second fix found mid-run is cheap to *write* and expensive to *ship*, and the deciding question is
whether it would otherwise be lost rather than whether it is small.

## 2026-10-14 (Builder, after merging v0.495.9) — the post-merge CI check that found a red `main`, and the §11 collision that then answered it better than I did

**Read this alongside the v0.495.10 note below it, which is the answer.** My run and that one found the same
red `main` within the hour; theirs root-caused and fixed it, mine got as far as "nondeterministic, mechanism
unidentified" and filed a lead. **Theirs is right and mine was wrong on the mechanism** — recorded rather than
quietly dropped, because the way I was wrong is reusable.

### What still stands: read `main`'s own CI run after merging, not just the PR's

They are different runs on different commits, and a PR's green does not speak for the merge commit's. `main`
run **2294** — the v0.495.9 merge commit — was red on
`tests/webapp/test_last_night.py::test_the_card_builds_no_frame_row_for_the_whole_library` (*"built 1 FrameRow
objects, assert 1 == 0"*), forty minutes after that PR had been green on all six checks. Both runs found it
this way. Had neither looked, AGENTS.md §2 would have handed the next run a red `main` as its first task with
no evidence attached.

Four cheap facts were worth gathering and are worth gathering again in this situation, because they close off
the *wrong* explanations even when they do not produce the right one: CI runs the suite **serially**
(`pytest tests/ -q`, read from `ci.yml`) so a shard layout cannot be the cause — and a local
`-n 4 --dist worksteal` pass therefore does not clear an ordering bug; the merge commit's tree was
**identical** to the PR head whose Python job passed; the same serial check passed on #1158, #1159 and `main`
run 2297; and the file was green locally 3/3 in isolation. One failure in five observations.

### Where I stopped, and why that was not good enough

I filed it as a lead with two candidate mechanisms — a failed `PUT /api/settings {site_lon}` reopening the
`SITELONG` frame-walk, and `detect_site_cached` crossing its TTL mid-request — and **both are wrong.**
v0.495.10 found the real one: `_row_to_frame` is a **module global**, `JobManager.stop()` signals its worker
without joining it, so a `job-worker` daemon thread from a *previous* test is still alive and its QC phase
builds exactly one `FrameRow` (`apply_qc_result_to_db` → `Project.get_frame`) — hence "built 1" rather than
"built 35894". The counter was measuring the **process**, not the surface.

**The lesson is about where I looked.** I treated "which code path inside this request could build a row?" as
the whole question, and the answer was that the row was not built by this request at all. *A process-global
patch in a shared-process suite has a third possibility beside "my code did it" and "flake": somebody else's
code did it, concurrently.* Enumerating that possibility costs one `threading.enumerate()` — which is exactly
what the other run did, and it named the thread.

My proposed next step (stash the first construction's traceback into the assertion message) was pointing the
right way and still short of the fix: the caller chain is not a nicer error message, it is the **measurement**
— `tests/framerows.py::frame_rows_built_by` counts a row only when a named call is on its own stack, so the
guard measures the surface and a stray row cannot reach it. Anchoring on `__code__` rather than a string, so a
rename cannot turn a guard into a tautology, is the detail worth copying.

### The §11 note, honestly

This is a collision of the kind this file keeps recording, and the sequence matters: I had no claim published
for it (I was mid-CI-wait on an unrelated docs PR when I read run 2294), so the other run had nothing to see.
Their fix landed as **v0.495.10** while my filing sat in CI. **Nothing of mine is re-applied on top** — the
Bugs entry I had written is dropped rather than merged, because an entry describing an open bug that is
already fixed is precisely the "backlog carries items already shipped" failure §1 warns about, and keeping it
would have cost the next run a grep. What survives is this note.

**And the one thing to carry into the next CI-wait:** a run that spots a red `main` should claim it *before*
investigating, not after it has something to say. Investigation is exactly the phase long enough for another
run to arrive, and the claim is the only thing that would have told either of us.

### The other flaky guard this run is unaffected

The `Editor.test.tsx` 1 s `findByText` finding (#1159) is a different mechanism — jsdom, no worker thread, a
testing-library timeout under CI load — and its entry stands as filed. Two flaky merge-gate guards in one run,
in both halves of the gate, was the observation; one of them now has a fix and the other does not.

## 2026-10-14 (Builder, branch `claude/relaxed-cray-fzxacq`) — `main` was red on a *test*, and the authority that said so was free

*(→ **v0.495.10**. Baseline: `main` at `89f01088` (v0.495.9), and its own CI run **2294** a **FAILURE** — one
test of 7,929, five of six jobs green. Inbox **four open**, confirmed with `list_issues`: #878, #880, #903,
#1015, every one previously acted-on and owner-gated, unchanged again. One open PR, **#1159**, docs-only from
the previous run's branch; the `--no-site` LEAD it files was ~30 minutes old when this run read it, i.e.
claimed-in-spirit under §11, and owner-data-gated besides. "Bugs" held nothing this repo can close and
"Features that serve real workflows" no open ready entry, so without the red CI this would have been a
dogfood run.)*

### Read `main`'s own CI conclusion before paying for a local baseline

The run opened by §2's habit — `git fetch`, read the two docs, `source scripts/agent-setup.sh`, start the full
suite — and on this box that suite is **~70 minutes, not the documented ~11** (4 cores, load pinned at 4.4
under `-n 4`, which is the right worker count here; the ~11 is someone else's box). At 15 % one
`mcp__github__actions_list` call on `ci.yml` filtered to `main` answered the same question in seconds and
answered it **differently**: run 2294 failed, with the failing test named in the job log. The local run was
killed.

**The rule worth keeping: `main`'s CI conclusion is the authority §8 names, it costs one call, and a local
baseline is the expensive way to re-derive it.** The two prior runs' notes argue about *ordering* a local
suite against a dogfood pass (2026-10-13, 2026-10-14); this is the cheaper question upstream of both — on a
run that starts with `origin/main` unchanged since the last CI push, the baseline is already computed.

### The failure, and why it was not about the code it accused

```
FAILED tests/webapp/test_last_night.py::test_the_card_builds_no_frame_row_for_the_whole_library
  - AssertionError: built 1 FrameRow objects for the Last-night card
```

`_collect_last_night` has read `Project.iter_night_frames` since v0.495.6 and builds **no** `FrameRow`. The
test passed alone here, passed under `-n 4` on the three local runs quoted in v0.495.6 – .9's own commit
messages, and passed on every PR check.

Established in this order:

1. `seestack.io.project._row_to_frame` is a **module global**, so `monkeypatch.setattr` of it sees every
   thread in the process.
2. **A `job-worker` outlives the `client` fixture** — two tests in one scratch file proved it:
   `client.post("/api/scan")` in the first, `threading.enumerate()` in the second →
   `['MainThread', 'job-worker']`. `webapp/main.py`'s lifespan calls `jm.stop()`, which sets `_stop` and
   pushes a queue sentinel but **never joins**, so a job already running finishes on its daemon thread,
   against the previous test's `tmp_path` (which still exists).
3. A scan builds exactly **one** `FrameRow` per frame through the only single-row reader in `Project`:
   `qc.runner.apply_qc_result_to_db` opens with `project.get_frame(result.frame_id)`. That is the `1`, and
   it is why the number was not 35,894.
4. **CI runs `pytest tests/ -q` sequentially in one process; the documented local command is
   `-n 4 --dist worksteal`.** Same collection order, four processes — so which neighbours precede a test, and
   how far they overlap it, is a different question in each place.

### Two false leads, recorded so nobody re-walks them

**Fixture contamination: ruled out.** `data_root`, `built_library` and `client` are all function-scoped on
`tmp_path`, so nothing accumulates across the tests of a file, and the xdist-distributes-a-file theory dies
with it. **Random ordering: ruled out** — `pytest-randomly` is not installed (`pytest`, `pytest-qt`,
`pytest-timeout`, `pytest-xdist`), so collection order is deterministic in both places.

**A direct repro did not fire, and that is consistent rather than disconfirming.** Submitting a 120-frame
scan in the test immediately before a copy of the counting test counted zero: the race needs one `get_frame`
to land inside one request's window, and a scan either finishes first or spends that window elsewhere. The
mechanism was established from its three independently-checkable parts instead, and the **fix** was then
tested against the part that matters — a row built on another thread.

### The generalisation, and the failure mode the fix had to avoid

A test that patches a shared seam is measuring the **process**, and a webapp test does not own its process.
So name the call: `tests/framerows.py::frame_rows_built_by` counts a row only when one of the named calls is
on its own caller chain.

The calls are passed **as objects** and matched on `__code__`, not by name, because the obvious stack-walk
has one bad failure mode of its own: an anchor that never matches makes the count zero for ever and the guard
passes **for the wrong reason** — silently, which is worse than the flake. An empty call list raises rather
than defaulting to "count everything", which is the bug being removed. And the anchoring is *measured*, two
ways, both through FastAPI's real `run_in_threadpool` hop: a scratch revert of `_collect_last_night` to
`iter_frames()` turns the converted test red, and `test_a_page_request_builds_only_that_pages_rows` still
asserts `built() == 1` — a non-zero expectation, which no silently-ignoring counter could satisfy.

### What was left alone, with the reason

`JobManager.stop()` still does not join. Joining would make a container stop — and every webapp test teardown
— wait out a running stack, and the leak is otherwise harmless: a daemon thread writing into a scratch
directory nobody reads again. Its only cost was to **process-global patches**, and the sweep for the rest of
that class in `tests/webapp` found exactly one other: `test_skipped_folders.py`'s two `scanner` stand-ins,
which *raise* — a leftover worker that hit one would fail its own job, not the test's assertion. The six
engine-side `_row_to_frame` counters in `tests/` (`test_project.py`, `test_project_night_frames.py`,
`test_project_health_frames.py`, `test_project_acquisition_values.py`, `test_project_frames_page.py`,
`test_session_recap.py`) build no app, so there is no worker to leak into them; they keep the plain counter.

## 2026-10-14 (Builder, same run as v0.495.9) — the `--no-site` pass: CLEAN, the fix verified in its second state, and one lead that the pass itself cannot evidence

### Why a second pass, and the gap it closed in my own work

v0.495.9 changes the behaviour of **two** pass-states — `--empty` and `--no-site` — and I had only ever run
`--empty`. That is the same shape as the bug it fixes (a guard never run against the flag whose premise it
breaks), so running the other one was not optional. **`--no-site` is CLEAN**: EXIT 0, *"nothing overflowing, no
console errors"*, the one `[note] /tonight: no view switch expected on this pass` firing correctly on a library
that *has* data but no site — which `--empty` could not have shown, since there the page is empty for two
reasons at once. Heights on the standing baseline (`[phone] /life-list [Still to shoot]` **14,513 px**, the
same figure the 2026-10-13 `--mosaic` pass recorded; `[phone] /glossary` 3,364).

**Carry forward: when a change alters what a flag prints, run every flag it alters.** The list is small and
mechanical — grep the constant you added for the pass-states that reach it — and it is exactly the step whose
absence created the bug being fixed.

### And the docs PR's own CI went red, which is the third record of this run

`Frontend build + tests` **failed on a docs-only PR** (#1159) — `Editor.test.tsx > EditorView > offers the
user's saved default recipe`, *"Unable to find an element with the text: Stretch"*. The diff touches four
`.md` files, and the identical frontend code had passed on #1158 **49 minutes earlier**, so it is not this
PR's. The temptation is to press re-run; what the rules ask for first is a root cause, and reading got one:
the file is 142 tests and **62.6 s locally** (green), three of its tests gate on
`await screen.findByText("Stretch")` at testing-library's 1 s default, and the comment directly above the
failing line records that a previous run *already* moved this wait once because gating elsewhere *"raced and
flaked in slower CI"*. **Second flake, same line, same shape** — filed with its evidence under "Bugs", not
fixed, because a timeout that only fires under contention cannot be given the §5 fail-before and raising the
constant on a hunch is a blind flip.

**The method note worth keeping: a red check on a diff that cannot have caused it is a finding about the
suite, not a reason to re-run.** Pressing re-run would have been correct by the letter of the flake rule (it
passed earlier on this exact code) and would have thrown away the one observation that makes it actionable —
that it is the *second* occurrence at that line. The cost of reading was five minutes.

### The finding, and the discipline of not filing it as a bug

Reading the Target-page paragraph as the probe asks produced a real pair: the readiness/grain card saying *"the
background already looks clean at 1 min (grain 0.001) … more time from here mostly buys fainter detail rather
than a visibly cleaner picture"*, and `/tonight`'s "Worth more time" card — *"ranked by how much another hour
on each would improve it"* — saying *"another hour would cut its noise about 87%"*.

**The numbers are both right**, which is the first thing to check and the thing that nearly made this a wrong
filing: 1 min → 2 min is a 29 % cut and 1 min → 61 min is 87 %, both exactly √N. So this is not an arithmetic
disagreement; it is a **verdict** disagreement, and the two surfaces reach it from different data.

**And the pass cannot evidence it.** σ 0.001 at one minute is a property of the synthetic sample (its lights
carry no hot pixels and no vignette — the `--calibration` caveat says so in as many words), not of the owner's
sky. A real one-minute stack would not measure clean, so the specific sentence pair on screen is a fixture
artefact. What survives that is the **mechanism**, traced in the code rather than read off the screen:
`nightplan._depth_component` is `noise_gain_from_more_time(total_exposure_s)` and nothing else, so the ranking
is structurally blind to the measured-σ verdict — and `grainProjection.ts`'s own comment says it took trouble
to stop *"'already looks clean' beside 'would clean up the background nicely'"* between **two** surfaces,
without noticing a third consumer of the same question.

So it is filed as a **LEAD with its gate named** ("count his targets that are clean-but-still-ranked; if zero,
close it with the measurement"), not as a reproduced bug. **The generalisable half: a fixture can show you a
true mechanism through a false number.** Keep the mechanism, throw the number away, and say in the entry which
is which — otherwise the next run reproduces the 87 % on the sample, calls it confirmed, and wires σ into a
library-wide hot path that v0.495.5–.7 have just finished taking reads *out* of.

## 2026-10-14 (Builder, branch `claude/relaxed-cray-4vizeh`) — DOGFOOD `--empty`, the stalest flag: one finding, and it was the instrument rather than the app

*(→ **v0.495.9**. Baseline: `main` at `23899a61`; the last **completed** CI run on `main` was green at
`54a2ef3a` (v0.495.7) and the two commits since are docs-only, HEAD's own run still in progress at the time.
Inbox **four open**, confirmed with `list_issues` rather than from `FOCUS.md` — #878, #880, #903, #1015, every
one previously acted-on and owner-gated, unchanged from the previous run's reckoning. One open PR, **#1157
holding v0.495.8**, which is why this run took 0.495.9 and not 0.495.8; it merged mid-run and was merged in
before the version was chosen.)*

### The §7 ordering rule paid out, in the direction the 2026-10-13 note warned about

I started the baseline suite out of §2 habit, read the backlog while it ran, concluded the queue was dry and
the §0 instruction ("do a dogfood pass and file what you find") applied — and had to **throw the suite away at
14 %** to run the dogfood, because the two cannot overlap. That is the 2026-10-13 record's lesson almost word
for word (*"when the run's plan contains a dogfood pass at all, the dogfood goes first"*), and it cost ~12
minutes this time rather than 20 because the same record's **other** number made the call easy: a suite
started in the same minute as `scripts/agent-setup.sh` crawls (~14 % in 12 min here, against a clean ~25 min
full run), so the run being abandoned was the slow one anyway. **The generalisable bit: the ordering rule is
not about the risk of a collision, it is about which artefact you are willing to pay twice for.** The
substitute baseline was the one §7 sanctions — CI's own green on `main`'s code — and the backlog read that
filled the wait was not wasted.

### Why `--empty` and not the others

Ranked by last *run*, not last mentioned: `--mosaic --editor --big` and `--deep` both ran **today**,
`--combine` yesterday, `--calibration`/`--incoming-lag` 2026-10-10, `--dithered` 2026-10-11, `--closing`
2026-10-13. `--empty` appears in the 2026-10-03 record **only as the name of a stale flag** ("the longest-unverified
flag alongside `--empty`") — it was not run — so its last real pass predates 2026-09-30. ~11 days, ~70
versions. A reading trap worth carrying: **grepping a flag's name in this file finds the run that called it
stale as readily as the run that ran it**, and the two read almost identically.

### The pass: mechanically clean, two findings, both the probe's own

Clean on every measure it takes — nothing overflowing, no console errors, the notice board carrying exactly
one note (*"Plate-solving isn't set up yet"*, the correct one for a first-run install, `1 of 1 speaking notes
visible without a click`), `/tonight` correctly prescribing nothing, and every page height on the standing
first-run baseline: `[phone] /glossary` **3,364 px** against 3,364, `[phone] /life-list [Still to shoot]`
14,604, `[desktop]` 5,236, `[phone] /settings/maintenance` 2,758.

`2 thing(s) to look at`, and both were `[desktop] /tonight` and `[phone] /tonight` reporting
*"NO VIEW SWITCH FOUND, but this page has one — … (a Mantine class rename?)"*.

**What settled it was the same pass's other rows, not the source.** `/life-list` is in the height table as
`[Still to shoot]`, i.e. its switch was found and clicked; `/logs` and `/sky` warned about nothing. So
discovery works and Mantine's class names are intact — the one explanation the message offered was the one
the pass itself disproved, three times over. The real answer is in `Tonight.tsx`: two early returns
(`location_source === "none"`, `!dark_window`) replace the entire planning body with an alert, and the switch
is the object-type filter **inside** that body. `--empty` never sets a site, by design.

### The method note: a guard whose premise is false on one flag, and the flag it was never run against

`KNOWN_VIEW_SWITCHES` landed **2026-09-30** (`de72b240`); `--empty` last ran **2026-09-26**. Those two dates
are the whole bug. A guard that exists to stop a sweep from silently covering less had spent two weeks
unable to produce anything *but* false findings on one flag, and nobody could have known, because the pass
that would have shown it is the pass nobody ran. **Generalisable: a guard added to this probe is untested
against every flag that was not run while it was being written — and `--empty` / `--no-site` are the two that
most often falsify an assumption, because they are the two where whole page bodies are absent.** When adding
a finding to `dogfood_probe.mjs`, run it under `--empty` before believing it, or say in its comment which
pass-states it has not met.

The probe's own docstring had predicted the *source*-side version of this (*"delete a SegmentedControl from
one of those pages and the probe starts crying wolf on every pass until someone reads the source"*) and
`tests/test_dogfood_view_switches.py` exists for it. Neither considered the **data** side, which needs no
code change at all to arrive.

### Two things checked rather than assumed, and both shaped the fix

1. **The precondition is the page's own, read from the app.** Asking `GET /api/plan/tonight` for
   `location_source !== "none" && dark_window` uses the two fields `Tonight.tsx`'s early returns read, rather
   than a second copy of the rule in the probe — the shape this repo has fixed drift in repeatedly. A test
   pins both fields against the page, so a page that stops gating on one of them goes red rather than leaving
   the exemption standing for a reason that no longer holds.
2. **Measured in both directions against a live app.** A scratch install on its own port: no site →
   `location_source=none`, no dark window → precondition **False** (exempt); after one `PUT /api/settings`
   with a site → `location_source=settings`, dark window present → **True** (the guard fires as before). That
   is what makes "every sited pass is byte-for-byte unchanged" a measurement rather than a claim — and it is
   the direction that mattered, because the risk of this change is exempting `/tonight` *everywhere*.

**A third thing, caught by re-reading my own diff rather than by a test, and it is the one worth copying.**
The first version of `ask()` returned `false` on a non-OK response — i.e. an unreachable or renamed
`/api/plan/tonight` would have *exempted* `/tonight` on every pass, silently, which is the exact failure the
guard exists to prevent and the opposite of what the docstring two lines above it promised. The adversarial
question that found it is cheap and general: **for a predicate that can grant an exemption, ask what each
failure path grants.** It now answers "met" for a throw *and* for a non-OK response, so only a successful
answer that genuinely says the control cannot render buys silence; a renamed endpoint reports instead of
hiding. Verified by re-running the pass (still exempt, still clean) — the live app answers 200 with
`location_source=none` on a first-run install, so the honest exemption goes through the success path.

**The third condition was deliberately not covered.** The control also needs ≥ 2 object-type buckets among
the targets clearing the minimum altitude (`typeOptions.length > 1`), which no honest precondition can ask
without re-deriving the page's bucketing. So the finding's wording now names **both** candidates ("a Mantine
class rename, or this pass's data not reaching the control") instead of asserting the one, and a sited pass on
a one-bucket night would still print it. Recorded rather than guessed at; cheap to tighten if such a pass is
ever seen.

### The re-run, which is the actual verification

The same `--empty` pass after the change: `nothing overflowing, no console errors`, one
`[note] /tonight: no view switch expected on this pass — …`, and **every** other figure identical to the run
before it (same eight heights, same single notice). Printing the lost coverage rather than swallowing it is
the half that keeps this from being a mute.

## 2026-10-14 (Builder, branch `agent/reveal-read-off-loop`, same run as v0.495.8) — a CLEAN dogfood record on the two stalest flags, a measured non-finding in Auto's apply-time curve, and the fix whose obvious version was 16× worse than the bug

**The dogfood record: `--closing --restack`, CLEAN.** The two stalest configurations (last run 2026-09-26 and
2026-10-05) in one pass, since they seed different states into one install and share a boot. Everything the
flags exist to reach was reached and said so: `location_source=settings` with `n_closing=2` and both rows
listed; the restack's two runs `#2/6 subs, #1/3 subs` (newest genuinely deeper, so no card is describing
"no change"), `[reel] available=True over 2 stack(s), 3 -> 6 subs` with `dated_by=capture`, and
`[noise-delta] available=True patch=160px pixel_exact=True ratio=1.658`. Page sweep: **"nothing overflowing,
no console errors"**, heights at the standing baseline (`[phone] /life-list [Still to shoot]` **14,513 px**,
identical to the last four records — and v0.492.2 already recorded that figure as *not* a bug, so it is a
control here and not a layout slice waiting to be taken). The three prescribing paragraphs read as one voice:
the Target page's coaching rung, framing verdict and readiness card all name the mosaic and the readiness card
carries its `for this single field` scope clause (v0.444.2), and on Tonight the week plan defers to the
closing card in the closing card's own words (v0.445.0). Nothing filed.

**A measured non-finding, recorded so nobody re-derives it.** `measured_region` (v0.494.5/v0.495.3) narrowed
every cue `auto_recipe` reads *at build time* to the rectangle the trim keeps. Two of Auto's ops instead derive
their numbers **at apply time**, from the image entering them — `tone.curves(auto=True)` via
`seestack/edit/curve.py` (`_sky_mode`, p50, p99.5) and `detail.sharpen`'s anchors — and Auto's `geometry.crop`
runs **last**, so at that moment the ragged fringe is still in the array. That is exactly the "callers the
migration stopped short of" shape, and it is **not** a bug: measured on the engine's own `_ragged` fixture at
four fringe bands (6/10/14/24 px, keeping 94.1 %/90.2 %/86.4 %/77.3 % of the canvas), the whole canvas and the
kept rectangle agree on the sky mode to **0.0003–0.005**, on p50 to 0.004 and on p99.5 to 0.002, and the
assembled curve points are identical to three decimals in three of the four bands (the 24 px band moves one
anchor by 0.003). The reason is structural rather than lucky: these are a *mode* and *percentiles* of a
population that is 77–94 % interior, where the v0.495.3 cues that did move were a mean-ish level and a σ. So
the general rule "narrow what Auto measures" does **not** extend automatically to apply-time measurements —
check the estimator's own robustness before filing one.

**The lesson from the fix, and it is about the obvious version.** The filed ⚪ said the honest next step was to
measure the stall; it was, and the stall is real (a `/api/health` call alongside four reveals waited 1,241 ms).
But the fix the entry named — `run_in_threadpool` on each read — measured **19,608 ms** for those four reveals
against **1,244 ms** for leaving the bug in place: these reads are slower in parallel than in series, because
`sqlite3` hands the GIL back around every row fetch and the convoy grows with the row count (three columns of
35,894 rows: 101 ms alone, 8,587 ms four-up; a row-less `count(*)`: 3 ms and 18 ms; four pure-Python loops of
the same length: 4.3×, i.e. just serialisation). **So "move the blocking work off the loop" is only half a
fix on a read that is row-bound** — the other half is a one-slot gate, and the shipped version is better than
both predecessors on both axes (1,145 ms for the four, 2.8 ms for the witness). Two generalisations worth
carrying: when a fix is a *concurrency* change, measure the thing being fixed **and** the thing it competes
with (here the user-visible latency of the very endpoints being helped, which the naive hop made 16× worse);
and a one-line diagnostic separates the explanations — a `count(*)` that moves no rows and a pure-Python loop
of the same duration told us it was the row traffic and not the GIL in general, which is what makes the gate
a measurement rather than caution.

## 2026-10-14 (Builder, same run as v0.495.6/v0.495.7) — a PR carrying two versions gets only the head one tagged

**What happened.** This run shipped two independently-green commits in one PR (#1154): `v0.495.6` then
`v0.495.7`. `Release tags` ran green on the merge and created **`v0.495.7` only** — `git tag -l 'v0.495.*'`
now reads `….2 .3 .4 .5 .7`, with a hole where 0.495.6 is.

**It is the workflow working as documented, not a failure.** `.github/workflows/release-tags.yml` tags "every
version transition on **main's first-parent line** since the last tag". A merge commit's first parent is the
previous `main`, so the PR's own commits sit on the *second* parent and are not on that line: the only
transition the walk sees is `0.495.5 → 0.495.7` at the merge. Nothing went red because nothing was reused or
moved backwards.

**What it costs, stated honestly.** Small, and it is not a reusable number: CI's `Version bump is sane` job
compares against `main`, which now reads 0.495.7, so no later PR can take 0.495.6 either. What is actually
lost is the tag's own job — `git checkout v0.495.6` cannot name the build that shipped it, and a rollback has
to name the merge commit or `v0.495.5`. `SHIPPED.md` and the PR carry the full description of both, so nothing
is unrecorded.

**The rule for next time.** **One version per PR.** Two versions in one PR is a deliberate trade — one CI
cycle instead of two (~50 minutes on this runner), paid for with a missing tag on the lower number. If both
tags matter, merge the first PR, then branch again from the new `main` for the second (AGENTS.md §11's warning
about a run's second PR competing with its own first applies: merge before opening it, and choose the second
number above whatever the first one shipped). This run took the single-PR trade because the two commits were
halves of one sweep and the second was finished while the first was still in CI; the note exists so the next
run makes that choice knowingly rather than discovering the hole afterwards. *(A `workflow_dispatch` backfill
of `release-tags.yml` is documented as "safe to re-run" and walks to the root — but it is a workflow run an
agent must not start on the owner's behalf, and AGENTS.md §8 is explicit that tags are written by workflows,
never by an agent, so this is recorded rather than repaired.)*

## 2026-10-14 (Builder, branch `claude/relaxed-cray-8ak3vj`, same run as v0.495.6) — the caller sweep is now a *method*, and two notes it produced

**The method, stated so it can be reused.** The previous run's note said that when a repo has measured a read
and built a cheap replacement, the next bug is in **the callers the migration stopped short of**. This run
applied it mechanically rather than by inspiration: `grep -rn 'iter_frames('` over `webapp/` and `seestack/`,
then for each hit ask only *"which fields does this caller actually read?"*. Thirteen hits; most are honest
(the stacker and QC want whole rows, `site_location` and `system.py` break out early, three in `stats.py`
and two in `frames.py` stream), and the cluster worth a version was the four night summaries. The sweep took
about twenty minutes and is repeatable on any `Project` read — `iter_stack_runs` is the obvious next one, and
it is *not* obviously wasteful (a `StackRunRow` has no `wcs_json`-sized column), which is why it was not
picked up here.

**Note 1 — a record earns its name from the set of consumers, not from the first one.** The task started as
"the Dashboard's last-night recap reads whole rows" (four fields), and the four-field record would have been
shipped had the sweep stopped there. Reading `session_recap.py`'s *other* whole-row readers turned up three
more surfaces wanting the same five fields, and three of those are on the Target page rather than the
Dashboard — a bigger win, found by widening the record by one field. The tell that the fifth field belonged
was that `_session_median_fwhm` is shared by two of the four already. So: before naming a reduced record,
grep its module for the other reads of the same table and see whether one record covers them; a record named
after one caller tends to need a sibling within a run or two.

**Note 2 — "three cards" is a different finding from "three endpoints".** The milliseconds here were never
going to carry a version on their own (1.7 s → 0.7 s on a cached-ish read). What did was reading the
*frontend*: `InsightTabs` renders every group and keeps the panels **mounted** on purpose — it measures which
cards produced DOM so an empty group gets no tab — so the three Target-page night cards are not alternatives,
they all fire on one view, and their peaks coincide (~437 MB → ~36 MB on the owner's deepest target). Same
shape as v0.495.4's lesson one level out: when a finding is about several surfaces, **go and read how the
page hosts them** before sizing it. A per-endpoint cost multiplies by however many of them one view mounts.

**Two smaller things, recorded rather than argued.**

* **The fail-before for a new *method* needs a path that does not name it.** `tests/test_project_night_frames.py`
  cannot even import against `origin/main` (no `_NIGHT_COLUMNS`), which is the trap `docs/AGENT-ENVIRONMENT.md`
  records for a new *module* showing up one level down. The honest fail-before is the no-row count taken
  **through the three public functions** and **through the endpoint** — `session_recap built 34 FrameRow
  objects`, `built 13 FrameRow objects for the Last-night card` — both verified in a `git worktree` at
  `origin/main` with `seestack.io.project.__file__` checked to be inside the worktree.
* **The endpoint-level "builds no row" assertion has a second reader in the request, and it is a feature.**
  The Last-night test first failed at `built 12`: with no configured site, `resolve_site_lon` sniffs
  `SITELONG` out of the subs' own headers and walks every accepted frame to do it (the bundled samples
  deliberately carry none). The test now sets `site_lon` first and says why. That read is a genuine third
  caller of the same shape, bounded by `max_probes` and breaking on the first readable path, so it was left
  alone — but it is the reason a whole-request row count is not the same claim as a function's.
* **Lint:** the two generic annotations added to `session_recap.py` (`_last_session_frames`,
  `recent_session_window_frames`) take that file's `UP047 non-pep695-generic-function` count from 2 to 4.
  Deliberate: the module already states its generics with `TypeVar` (`_TimedT`, right above the first of
  them), PEP 695 syntax appears nowhere in this repo, and the alternative was an annotation that names a
  record the function is no longer only called with. Every other rule's count on all three touched files is
  byte-identical to `main`'s.
