  3×3; 1 min of ~2 h, a good start; no darks but the background measures clean, so darks would mostly tidy
  hot pixels; the framing verdict's own 9-panel arithmetic). Nothing guessing at what a sibling had measured
  — which is the class the last four findings came from.
* The expected side effect happened and is not a finding: the deep target is the deepest thing in the
  scratch library, so `/tonight`'s week plan names it for every night. The flag's own header says to read
  that column on an ordinary or `--mosaic` pass.

**The one thing worth carrying is what the pass could NOT do.** This run filed a ⚪ about both reveal
handlers doing their project read on the event loop, and wrote its gate as *"measure whether a Jobs or
History page at his depth shows the stall in a real browser — `--deep` is the flag with the row counts"*.
Running it showed that gate is unreachable: **`--deep` deliberately leaves the deep target unstacked** (its
own comment: *"1,200 subs is a stack nobody in a scheduled run will wait for, and nothing this flag exists to
measure needs a picture"*), so that target has **no stack run** — so `StackNoiseBadge` and
`OneFrameVsStackCard` never mount on it, and the two handlers in question are never called at scale by any
flag in this repo. The entry's gate is corrected to say so.

**Generalisation:** a flag's *documented omission* is as load-bearing as what it loads. Before writing "X is
gated on `--flag`", check that the flag reaches the **surface**, not just the magnitude — a sample sized for
one cost can be structurally unable to exhibit a different one. The same shape as the `--deep` header's own
warning that it scales with frame **count** and not with pixels, one level up: this one does not scale with
*runs* at all.

## 2026-10-14 (Builder, branch `claude/brave-albattani-gqf5wp`) — v0.495.5: the read nobody had followed to its other callers, and what "bugs first" means on a dry Bugs section

*(Baseline `main` green at `7a862c55`: **7908 passed, 7 skipped** in **18m39s** with `-n 4 --dist worksteal`
and the BLAS cap, on a 4-core box; CI run 2276 green on that exact commit. No open PRs. Inbox: the same four
open issues, every one already acted on and owner-gated — nothing to do there this run.)*

**How the task was found, which is the part worth carrying.** "Bugs (fix these first)" held nothing
reproduced and §2's big-picture dogfood was paid the day before, so the usual two doors were both shut. The
door that was open was neither the backlog nor a dogfood: it was **reading the consumers of a measurement
this repo has already made.** `Project.iter_health_frames` carries two measured numbers in its own docstring
(1,180 ms / 144.0 MB → 541 ms / 9.8 MB on 35,894 subs) and `FrameHealth` carries a sentence saying
`sky_adu_median` is on it *"for the reference-sub pick that rides along on the same read"*. Both were written
for the Target page's health card in v0.471.x/v0.475.1. Grepping for the *other* callers of that pick found
four endpoints that had never been moved onto it — and the pure function in the middle
(`reference_sub_from_frames`) even documents that it accepts either kind of record, which is how the two
halves came to disagree without anyone noticing.

**Generalisation:** when a repo has measured a read and built a cheap replacement, the bug is often not in
the read or the replacement but in **the callers the migration stopped short of**. `grep` for the helper the
measurement names, not for the symptom. The tell here was a docstring that described a capability
("a caller may hand it `FrameHealth` records as readily as whole rows") that no caller used.

**The second tell, and the one that turned a cheaper read into a finding worth a version: the cache that was
supposed to make this page cheap did not cover it.** The noise badge's ratio is stamped so repeat views don't
reload the master — but the stamp is fingerprinted on the representative sub's **id**, and the only way the
endpoint had to learn that integer was the whole-row sweep. So every *cached* view paid 153 MB and 1.5 s to
look up a number it already had. A cache is worth reading twice: once for what it saves, and once for **what
it still has to compute in order to use it**.

**And the magnitude only became a priority once the mounts were read.** 153 MB on one request is a number;
`StackNoiseBadge` mounted on `Target.tsx` (every view), again on `Jobs.tsx` once per run shown, and
`OneFrameVsStackCard` on `History.tsx` firing two queries per run card, is a page that can ask for it several
times over. That is the same method note v0.495.4 recorded — **go and read how the host mounts/ranks the
thing before sizing it** — applied to cost rather than to wording.

**On the fail-before.** Reverting the fix outright makes `tests/test_reference_sub_read_cost.py`
*uncollectable* (it imports the new `_reference_sub_row`), and an import error is a weaker proof than an
assertion: it says the name is missing, not that the behaviour was wrong. So the scratch revert put back only
the pick's two lines and left the new helper in place — and all three tests then failed on their own
assertions: *"the pick peaked at 2673 KiB against 2652 KiB for the same frames as rows"*, *"built a FrameRow
for every sub of the target"*, and `assert ['rows'] == []`. Worth doing that way round whenever a fix adds a
symbol as well as changing a behaviour.

**One thing deliberately not built, filed instead** (⚪ in Bugs): both `async` handlers here do the whole
project read on the **event loop** while carefully putting the pixels in a threadpool, so the frame read
blocks every other request — 719 ms at his depth even after this fix. Moving one read would make two handlers
disagree with every neighbour in the file for no visible reason, and moving all of them is the speculative
refactor §10 forbids; the honest next step is a `--deep` pass in a real browser to see whether the stall
shows, which is a number nobody has.

## 2026-10-13 (Builder, branch `claude/brave-albattani-32mwni`) — the §2 big-picture dogfood on its stalest flag, and a §7 ordering mistake that cost 20 minutes

*(→ **v0.495.4**. Baseline: **CI run 2274 green on `main` at `c800574c`**, no open PRs, inbox four open and
every one already acted-on and owner-gated — unchanged from the previous run's reckoning.)*

### The §7 ordering mistake, which is the part worth writing down

`docs/FOCUS.md` said the one-run-in-three whole-journey dogfood was owed, so the plan was always a dogfood
pass. I started the **baseline `pytest` first anyway**, out of §2's start-of-run habit, and then had to throw
it away 20 minutes in: `docs/AGENT-ENVIRONMENT.md` §7 says *"dogfood first, `pytest` after"*, and on a fresh
checkout the collision is not a risk but a certainty — **`webapp/static/` does not exist at all**, so
`agent-dogfood.sh` is guaranteed to run `npx vite build`, and `emptyOutDir: true` empties the directory every
`create_app()` fixture reads. The two cannot overlap, and the suite was going to take ~2 h on this box (4
cores, ~16 % in 20 min) and then be invalidated anyway by the fix that followed.

**The rule to carry: when the run's plan contains a dogfood pass at all, the dogfood goes first, before the
baseline suite — not just "not at the same time".** §2 and §7 read as if the baseline comes first and a
dogfood is slotted in later; on a run whose *task* is the dogfood, that ordering costs a whole suite. What
stood in for the baseline is the signal §7 itself recommends as the independent one: **`main`'s own CI run on
the exact HEAD commit**. That is a real green suite on this code, not an assumption, and it is the only thing
that made abandoning the local one honest rather than convenient. Worth saying plainly so the next run does
not read this as licence to skip a baseline: it is licence to *substitute CI's green on the same commit*, and
only when the local suite physically cannot run yet.

### The pass: `--combine`, chosen because it was the stalest flag there is

Last run **2026-09-30** at v0.491.x — ~45 versions and 13 days back, where `--mosaic --editor` has been run
four times in the last week. It is also the only configuration that starts where the owner's data starts and
the only one that fingerprints `incoming/` for §10.

**CLEAN, mechanically, including §10.** EXIT 0. After the whole journey: *"all 7 original file(s) still
there, unchanged"*, the one sub the pass drops in itself listed as create-new. The merge carried 3 frames and
kept 1 picture, its notes arrived **attributed** (`From "M 31_night_2": …` — v0.491.1's own fix, still
holding), `merge-suggestions` offered the group at 0.0 arcmin once both targets had a centre, two rescans held
the combine at one 7-frame target, and a further night dropped into the folder that was combined away landed
in the **deep** target. 53 desktop + 54 phone page shots, *"nothing overflowing, no console errors"*. The one
`ERROR`/`Traceback` in the server log is step 3's deliberate pre-solve stack refusal.

### The finding, and why reading the paragraph is what found it

It is the fifth-or-so finding in a row of the class the probe's own instructions name, and the **2026-09-30
`--combine` record predicted exactly where it would be**: *"a `--combine`/`--merge` pass has to be read for
what the app says once the operation is over, not only for whether the operation worked."* Nothing mechanical
was wrong this time either.

Target page, inline: *"This stack combined only 3 frames — very few, so it will still look noisy. **Check that
your subs plate-solved and weren't over-rejected** (see the "rejected" count above), **then add more subs**."*
Beside it: *"**3 subs missing from your current picture** … it's thinner than your own data. **Restack**."*
Both halves of the first are wrong about the same subs — they *did* solve and were *not* rejected, which is
why the second can count them — and he need not shoot anything.

**What made it worth a version rather than a note is the ranking, and that took reading `NoticeBoard` rather
than the two sentences.** The board keeps `inlineCount = 2` of the *speaking* notes inline **by priority**: the
thin-stack warning is `NOTICE_PRIORITY.warning` (20), the corrective note is `advisory` (30). So the guess wins
an inline slot and the measured remedy sits behind *"N more notes"* — and the pass's own output says that fold
is the normal case (*"2 of 4 are visible without a click — the folded ones are what the page does NOT say to a
reader who never expands it"*). The warning also **suppresses** `NextBestMoveBadge` (`!thinStack`), under a
comment saying the two must not both nudge "add more subs", so in that state it is the page's single "what
next" voice. **A disagreement between two notes is worth a different amount depending on which of them the
page shows first** — that is the generalisable half, and no reading of either sentence reaches it.

### Two things that were checked rather than assumed, and both constrained the fix

1. **Which run each number is about.** `thinStack` describes `latestRun`; `newSubsSinceStack` is
   `new_light_since_picture`, measured against the run behind the **displayed** picture, which may be a pinned
   cover. Pairing them naively would have been the same substitution bug this repo has fixed four times. The
   figure is therefore passed **only** when `pictureRun.id === latestRun.id`.
2. **The stand-down recorded under v0.491.1** — *"making the analysis follow a pinned cover is the change that
   comment exists to refuse"* — and `Target.tsx`'s own comment saying `latestRun` deliberately stays the newest
   run. Neither is touched: the warning still describes the latest run, and the gate above is what keeps that
   true rather than quietly re-opening the question. **A stand-down nearby is not the same as a stand-down on
   your item**; the way to tell is whether your change makes the refused thing happen, and here it does the
   opposite.

Two cases fall out right for free, which is usually the sign the gate is in the right place:
`newSubsSinceStack` is zeroed on purpose while `needsProcessing` or `solveSetup` hold — and when plate-solving
genuinely is not set up, *"check that your subs plate-solved"* is precisely the correct advice, so the reader
keeps it.

### Fail-before, and what the tests that passed before are for

10 new tests, **5 fail before** (both source files reverted in place and re-run, including the page-level
*"names the restack"*). The other 5 pass before **by design** and are the more interesting half: they pin the
byte-for-byte degrade across `null`/`undefined`/`0`/`-2`/`0.4`/`NaN`, the wall card's pointer, the depth claim
itself, and the two stand-downs (no count waiting; an older cover on show). On a change whose whole risk is
"did you move a sentence three other surfaces share", the tests that must pass **both** before and after are
what bound the blast radius, and a fail-before count alone would have understated the work.

### Numbers for the next run

* Full Python suite on this box at `-n 4 --dist worksteal` with the BLAS cap: **7908 passed, 7 skipped in
  25:09** — in line with the 2026-09-30 record, so nothing to worry about. **And a correction worth having,
  because I nearly filed the wrong number:** the run I abandoned was crawling (~16 % in 20 min, which
  extrapolated to ~2 h) and the cause was not the box — it was `scripts/agent-setup.sh`'s `npm install` and
  toolchain work still competing for the same 4 cores. **Do not benchmark the suite against a run started in
  the same minute as setup**, and do not record a timing from one; the clean run was 5x faster.
* `npx vitest run`: **300 files / 4664 tests**, ~50 min on the same box. `vite build` 20.6 s.
* `--combine` baseline, for comparison with the 2026-09-30 one: 53 desktop / 54 phone shots, tallest page
  `[phone] /life-list [Still to shoot]` **14,513 px** (unchanged from the 2026-10-13 `--mosaic` pass's own
  14,513), `[phone] /tonight` 3,368 px, `[phone] /targets/<T>/edit/<run>` 3,299 px.

## 2026-10-13 (Builder, branch `claude/brave-albattani-totnig`, after the merge) — §11 miss: v0.495.3 was built for two hours with no published claim

Recording my own deviation, because this is the collision class §11 exists for. §2 says *"mark it **In progress**
in the backlog with your branch in the commit that starts it"*; I went straight from choosing the
`auto_crop`-OFF remainder to measuring it, and the entry only ever appeared in the record as Shipped. No
collision happened — `origin/main` did not move for the whole run — so nothing was lost, but for roughly two
hours a second run reading "Bugs" top-down would have seen that entry unclaimed and could have spent its whole
run on the same measurement.

**What made it easy to skip, and the cheap fix.** The claim is owed *"in the commit that starts the work"*, and
this task's first two hours produced **no commit at all** — it was two scratch scripts and a sweep, with the
first repo edit coming only once the decision was made. A measurement-first task therefore has no natural hook
for the claim, which is exactly when the claim is most useful: a run that is *measuring* an entry is the one
whose work is invisible to everybody else. **So: on a task whose first phase is a measurement, push the claim
line as its own `docs:` commit before the first scratch script**, not with the first code change. It costs one
commit and it is the only thing that makes a two-hour measurement visible.

## 2026-10-13 (Builder, branch `claude/brave-albattani-totnig`) — the gate that was "waiting on a number" had the number inside the repo, and the measurement answered a question nobody had asked

**The run.** Baseline `origin/main` at `cc8265f2` green (**7904 passed, 7 skipped** in 20:19), CI green, no open
PRs, inbox four open and all previously acted-on and owner-gated (#1015, #903, #880, #878 — no new observer
issue since #1120, which is closed). "Bugs (fix these first)" held nothing reproduced, exactly as the previous
two notes said. One task shipped: **v0.495.3**, the remainder of the `auto_crop`-OFF lead.

**The method note worth carrying, because it is the second run in a row to find this.** The previous note said:
*"when a gate names an instrument, check first whether the quantity it is reaching for is already measured
somewhere."* This entry named a **quantity** rather than an instrument — *"how far the target grey moves when
the fringe is excluded from the measurement but kept in the render"* — and it had been read for two weeks as
owner-data-gated company to the two LEADs beside it. It is not: the engine's own `_ragged` fixture builds that
exact canvas, `auto_recipe(auto_crop=…)` is the only difference between the two candidate behaviours, and
stripping the crop op from the trim-**on** recipe gives the proposed behaviour exactly, with no new code at
all. Two scratch scripts and about twenty minutes. **The tell for "this gate is cheaper than it reads" is that
the two behaviours differ by one argument of one pure function** — then the measurement is a loop, not a
build.

**And the measurement did not answer the question the entry asked.** The entry framed it as a size — how far
does the grey move, is it enough to be worth churn — and the size (2.3 % at a 5.9 % fringe, 10.6 % at 39.7 %)
is not what settles it. What settles it is that the **kept rectangle's sky level is flat in the fringe width
while the whole canvas's climbs with it**: same scene, same sky, three fringe bands, and one of the two numbers
moves by a factor of two. That makes it a question about *which number is about the sky* rather than about
whether a difference is big enough to care, and the "but the fringe is in the rendered picture" argument the
gate rested on does not survive it — the fringe renders at 0.13–0.17 grey under **both** cue sets, nowhere near
either stretch target, so the measurement it was buying never aimed at it. **A difference-of-two-answers
measurement is worth an invariance sweep as well as a magnitude**: if one candidate is invariant to a knob that
should not matter and the other is not, that is a stronger finding than any effect size, and it is cheap
(three canvases).

**The validating dogfood pass (`scripts/agent-dogfood.sh --mosaic --editor`, after the fix): CLEAN — and it
is a control, not evidence.** Both page sweeps "nothing overflowing, no console errors", mosaic trim 7.9 %, the
panel map agreeing with the health sentences, 21/21 editor ops previewed with undo/redo on both samples, both
chip classes behaving, and the mosaic's own "What Auto-process did" naming nine steps ending in the trim.
**That last clause is why it is a control**: the bundled samples run with `auto_crop_border` **on**, which is
the path this change leaves byte-identical, so a clean pass confirms nothing regressed and says nothing about
the path that moved. Worth knowing before a future run reads "dogfood clean" as validation of a trim-off
change: no bundled sample exercises the preference off, and `measured_region`'s own note explains why one that
did would still be blind (the `--mosaic` sample's fringe is 3.1 % of its finite population and its `target_bg`
sits on a clamp). The trim-off path's evidence is the 160-canvas sweep and the endpoint test, not the browser.
`/life-list [Still to shoot]` is **14,513 px** on phone, unchanged from the previous two passes' baseline — a
known number, still nobody's reported friction, and still the one measured-long page if a run ever wants §1's
layout slice.

**One mechanical thing, for a run that touches this family again.** `test_auto_crop_off_changes_nothing_else_about_the_recipe`
(`tests/test_edit_engine.py`) has asserted the **new** behaviour all along — `off_ops == on_ops[:-1]` — and
passed under the old gate only because its fixture is a 48×64 uniform-noise patch whose narrowing cannot move a
snapped param. A test whose fixture cannot express the behaviour it names is green for the wrong reason in both
directions; the same shape is why this file's own `_scene(mosaic=True)` could not see the border bug that
started this chain (v0.492.49), and why `_ragged` exists.

**#1120 is closed and the inbox is down from five to four**, so the previous two notes' "five open" is stale.

**The method note, and it is the transferable part.** The item this run shipped had been gated for weeks on
*"that is a measurement on a real browser rather than a reading of the code"*. The measurement that settled it
was neither in a browser nor about the number the gate named. The gate assumed the question was *"is 600 ms
right?"*; the answer turned out to be *"what does one render of the recipe Auto actually emits cost, per canvas
size?"* — **286 ms** on a single field, **5.08 s** on an owner-shaped 1693×1150 mosaic proxy, with **no `heavy`
op in either**. Once that is on the page the constant is unanswerable on purpose: the same canvas is a different
number of seconds on a different box, so the honest fix measures at runtime. Two artefacts already held most of
it — `webapp/edit_resume_cache.py`'s own table, and the running app's own "What Auto-process did" sentence naming
which ops Auto chose on the bundled mosaic. **So when a backlog entry names an instrument it is waiting for,
check first whether the quantity it is reaching for is already measured somewhere in the repo, and whether the
honest answer is "no constant can know this" rather than a better constant.** That is the same shape as the
2026-10-13 note below about a design call being a Builder's to make: the gate was about judgement, not data.

**The mistake this run actually made, and it cost a CI run.** I cancelled PR #1149's first, perfectly healthy
CI run after about **four minutes**, having convinced myself it had been stalled for two hours. The arithmetic
was invented: I had issued a series of *backgrounded* waits, which return to the agent immediately, and then
counted them as elapsed wall clock while polling the checks. Four jobs really were green in 90 s; the other two
were simply still running, on exactly their normal schedule (frontend unit tests take ~8m24s on this repo,
Python tests ~46m). The signs I read as "the control plane lost the runners" — a frozen `updated_at`, a `cancel`
that had not taken effect, a `pip install` "stuck" — were all just a run that was 4 minutes old.
**The rule: never call a job stalled without comparing `date -u` to its own `started_at`, and know that a job
has a normal duration worth looking up first** (`list_workflow_jobs` on the previous run of the same workflow
prints every step's start and finish). A backgrounded wait is not a passage of time. And `rerun_workflow_run`
answering *403 This workflow is already running* is a hint that the run is alive, not that it is wedged — the
only way to get a fresh run then is a **real** push to the branch, never an empty commit, which is what this
note is.

**One mechanical trap worth the line.** `@mantine/hooks`' `useDebouncedValue` lists `wait` in its effect's
dependency array, so **changing the delay re-arms a pending timer**. Any future "adaptive" delay in this
codebase has to be quantised for that reason alone — a value that tracked a measurement's jitter would keep
restarting the settle the user is already waiting on. It is why v0.495.2 is a three-rung ladder and not an
arithmetic expression, and the ladder's own promise ("2.4 s and 3.1 s agree") is pinned by a test.

## 2026-10-13 (Builder, branch `claude/brave-albattani-0rmc6t`) — the owner-answered item built; the prerequisite bug found by *reading the spec against the code*; and one optional keyword that broke 41 tests

*(Baseline `origin/main` at `f4a153b3` (0.494.5): CI green on `main`'s head, **no open PRs**, issue inbox
holding the same five previously-acted-on, owner-gated issues (#1120, #1015, #903, #880, #878) — nothing new.
"Bugs (fix these first)" ungated-and-undecided: still nothing. So the task was the one the previous run's
FOCUS note had already named: the ⭐ owner-answered entry at the top of "Features that serve real workflows",
whose answering PR #1143 had merged a few hours earlier. **Final: 7896 passed, 7 skipped, 16m44s**; `tsc`,
4,642 vitest tests and `vite build` green; dogfood CLEAN.)*

**The transferable finding: read the spec's own mechanism against the code before building the surface.** The
owner's answer names the opt-out mechanism in a parenthesis — *"a per-target saved `drizzle: false`, **which
already wins**"* — and in the engine it does: `walkaway.drizzle_choice_expressed` reads the key's *presence*,
so an explicit `false` stands the target down. In the **endpoint that writes it**, it did not. `Save as
defaults` has stored only what the form *changed* since v0.374.0, `drizzle`'s engine default is also `false`,
and v0.494.0 added the presence rule without adding the key to `put_stack_defaults`' `always_persist` tuple —
so the delta dropped exactly the value that carries the decision. The button the spec describes would have
been a no-op shipped with tests that each passed, because the natural tests (does the endpoint write it? does
the engine honour it?) both pass; what fails is the third one nobody writes — *does it survive the next press
of the form that owns the blob?* **When a spec says "X already wins", check the writer as well as the reader.**

**And the shape that made it invisible: a list spelled out at the call site.** The rule lives in
`walkaway.py`; the list of keys it needs lived as a literal in `routers/stack.py`
(`always_persist=(*AUTO_REJECT_OPT_KEYS, "drizzle_reject")`). v0.494.0 edited the rule and never saw the list.
It is now one constant, `PRESENCE_IS_THE_CHOICE`, beside the rule, and the endpoint reads it — which is the
same move as v0.494.4's "a docstring that names a second owner of the rule you are changing is naming your
second edit", one level down: **a literal list at a call site is a second owner of a rule, and a silent one.**

**One optional keyword, 41 failing tests, and a failure message that named none of it.** `run_stack` gained
`on_auto_drizzle=None` — optional, defaulted, and passed unconditionally from `_stack_target`. Every
`tests/webapp` test that stubs `run_stack` writes the signature out in full, so **17 files** needed `**_kw`.
Grepping `def fake_run_stack(proj, opts, *, progress=None, cancel=None,` found 17 of them and **missed
`test_reprocess_all.py`, whose stub is called `fake` and spells the signature on one line** — so the full
suite came back with 40 failures reading `reprocess-all: target M_42 failed` and nothing else: the
`TypeError: fake() got an unexpected keyword argument` is swallowed by the batch's own per-target isolation.
**The fix for next time is the sweep, not the grep**: parse every
`monkeypatch.setattr("seestack.stack.stacker.run_stack", <name>)`, find `<name>`'s `def`, and assert `**` is in
its signature. That script is five lines, found all of them, and is the check to run *before* the full suite
whenever a hot-path engine entry point gains a parameter. Grepping one spelling of a signature is not it.

**A mid-run edit's phantom failures, confirmed again — and the cheap way to tell.** The first baseline came
back `2 failed` in `tests/webapp/test_derived_light.py`, a file this run never touched; both passed in
isolation moments later, and neither appeared in either later full run. The cause is the documented one (source
files edited while the suite was running — AGENTS.md §7), and the useful detail is the **tell**: a phantom
failure is in a file your diff does not name, and it does not reproduce. A *real* one from the same run was in
a file the diff does not name either (`test_reprocess_all.py`), and **did** reproduce. So "re-run the file
alone" is the whole discriminator, and it costs 30 seconds.

**A measurement published once, read in one place.** `DRIZZLE_COST_RATIO` in
`seestack/stack/autodrizzle.py` is the ×7.3 / ×2.9 from `scripts/measure_drizzle_cost.py`, and
`tests/test_auto_drizzle_cost_note.py` asserts it still equals `5.68 / 0.78` and `2.23 / 0.78` to 2 %. That
test exists so the next person to re-run the instrument changes one constant and sees the assertion that tells
them where the number is consumed, rather than finding a second copy of ×7 in a docstring somewhere.

**Dogfood CLEAN** (default pass, run before `pytest` as §7 requires): nothing overflowing, no console errors,

## 2026-10-13 (Builder, branch `claude/hopeful-dijkstra-06a17n`) — the lead that named its own missing evidence, and the half of its fix that lived in the engine

*(Baseline `origin/main` at `00ca05d6` (0.494.4): **7870 passed, 7 skipped**, 18m43s, `-n 4 --dist worksteal`;
CI green on `main`; **no open PRs**. Issue inbox: five open, every one already acted on and owner-gated — and
#1015's own "suggested fix" (*put the app version in `/api/health`*) was **checked in the code before anything
else** and is shipped, which is the cheapest thing an unattended run can get wrong by trusting an issue's age.
So the frontier was "Bugs (fix these first)" again, and the choice came from reading the entries for the one
whose own text names evidence nobody had gathered.)*

**How this run's task was chosen, which is the transferable part.** Three previous runs read "Bugs" as
"gated-or-decided" and reached for a dogfood pass. That reading is right about the *headlines* and wrong about
the *bodies*: the `auto_crop`-OFF archetype LEAD ends with a parenthesis naming the cheap measurement that
would settle it, and no run had taken it. **An entry filed as "M to decide" is not the same as an entry that is
waiting on the owner** — the decision is a Builder's to make once the number exists, and the entry says which
number. Worth re-reading the bodies of the gated entries for that shape before concluding a section is dry.

**The measurement, and why one parameterisation would have been the wrong answer.** Over the engine's own
`_ragged` four-panel canvases, **9 fringe bands × 8 seeds × 5 σ = 360**, the whole canvas and the kept
rectangle disagree on **5** — all five at a trim of **15.4 % or more**, none below, and all five at σ = 0.02.
A first pass (5 bands × 6 seeds × 2 σ = 60) found 3, and would have supported the same conclusion for a
slightly wrong reason: it had no case at all between 13.6 % and 22.7 %, so it could not see that the boundary
sits just about where AGENTS.md's own "above ~15 % is a bug, not a ragged edge" line is. **The v0.492.54
docstring's figure for the same comparison is "8 of 30, the cheapest at 13.6 %"**, which is a different
parameterisation of the same harness and a reminder that the *rate* here is a property of the sweep; what is
robust, and what the decision rests on, is the **direction** — every differing case is a confident
whole-canvas `cluster` (0.82–0.84) against a kept-rectangle *nothing*, on 360 canvases as on 30.

**The reasoning that turned a rate into a decision.** Not "5 of 360 is a lot" — it is not — but that the
whole-canvas verdict is **never** the better one, so the change is monotone. The gate was conflating *which
pixels are in the picture* with *which pixels should set a global noise threshold*; `classify_target`'s
threshold is a global `6·sky_sigma`, so fringe grain hides faint structure in the **interior** too. A rule to
carry: **when a gate makes one region answer two questions, ask whether either answer is ever improved by the
gate.** If one of them never is, the rate stops being the argument.

**The half that was nearly missed, and the tell.** `webapp.routers.editor` has three archetype call sites and
they were the obvious diff. But `presets.auto_recipe` **classifies for itself** (it is what resolves
`object_type` for `auto_knob_values`) off its own `auto_crop`-gated region — i.e. the *read* side of the taste
profile lives in the engine while the *write* side lives in the webapp. Fixing only the webapp would have
re-created the exact write/read disagreement v0.492.54 exists to stop, from the other direction, and every
webapp test would have been green. **The tell was in v0.492.54's own docstring** — it says the bucket must
agree with "the archetype `auto_recipe` itself keys on", which is a statement that `auto_recipe` has one of its
own. A docstring that names a *second* owner of the rule you are changing is naming your second edit.

**Five tests re-reasoned, and the check that it was not a weakening.** Each had asserted the old gate in its
docstring, so each had to say the opposite — which is the shape AGENTS.md warns about. The discipline used:
every rewrite asserts something *stronger* (an invariance across all four spellings of the preference rather
than one value of it), the control that must not move was written down as its own test
(`test_the_border_trim_preference_still_gates_every_cue_that_sets_pixels`), and the fail-before was taken by
restoring both production files from `HEAD` and running the eight: **7 failed, 1 passed**, the one being that
control. A set of re-reasoned tests where *every* member fails before is a warning sign, not a good one — it
means nothing in the set is pinning what stayed put.

**And the `measured_region` identity test was the one not to touch.** `test_with_auto_crop_off_the_whole_canvas
_is_classified_again` looked like a sixth test to invert; it is not — it asserts `measured_region`'s own
behaviour (handed no rectangle, narrow nothing), which did not change. Only its docstring's claim about "the
recipe's rule" did. Renamed and re-worded, assertion untouched.

backlog's "Live preview" entry still lists responsiveness as open, and the spec for the next bite lives next to
the measurement that chose the last one.

### The method note: the stand-down was right, and it was right about the *instrument*, not the idea

v0.382.2 declined to replay a recorded **field** because the reconstruction is
`before + float32(after − before)`, which is not `after` — ~4e-7 of float32 rounding, on the one surface whose
job is to show what the export will do. Three runs of this repo's own history say a near-miss on a priority-1
parity surface is not worth taking, so the refusal stands. What it did not ask is whether the *saving* needs
the field at all. It does not: the thing worth keeping is the **picture at the boundary**, and an array handed
back to a deterministic pipeline is exactly what the pipeline would have produced. So the same 1.8× came back
**bit-identical** (max diff exactly 0 on four canvases, three of them mosaics with 3.6–4.8 % uncovered), with
*one* array instead of two fields, and with no engine change at all — because the split is made where no
stretch has run, so two ordinary `apply_recipe` calls compose into what one call does.

**Transferable:** when a measured stand-down turns on a *property of the mechanism* (here, that reconstructing
a value from a float32 delta loses a rounding), check whether the goal needs that mechanism before accepting
the price or the refusal. The entry had already priced the only instrument it considered.

And the second half, which cost the first version of the budget: **the question "how much memory is this?" has
a different answer per canvas, so the bound has to be in bytes.** An entry count bounds a store of scalars
(v0.382.2's eight slots are kilobytes); it bounds nothing when a slot is an image — two slots is 12 MB on the
`--mosaic` sample and 54 MB on the largest proxy the editor can build.

## 2026-10-12 (Builder, the auto-drizzle run) — "the spec named two different numbers in one sentence"

The method note behind **v0.494.0**, and it is about reading a spec rather than reading code.

**An owner-approved spec can still contain a contradiction, and the right move is to resolve it in writing
rather than to pick the nearer half.** The auto-drizzle spec's "when" clause said *"depth per output pixel
≥ 200 subs — measured **per panel** on a mosaic, the same per-pixel count `samplesPerPixel` /
`DRIZZLE_MIN_SAMPLES_PER_PIXEL` use, never the target total"*. Those are two different numbers:
`samplesPerPixel` reads `pixel_depth` (canvas area ÷ frame footprint) and **explicitly not** `panel_depth`
(the thinnest substantial pointing cluster), for a measured reason — `panel_depth` came out ~0.10× the real
per-pixel depth on 12 of 17 of the owner's mosaics and once went the *other* way, which is how the Stack form
came to tell him to turn Drizzle off on six pictures measured 117–153 subs deep (observer issue #901). So the
parenthetical wins over the adjective, and `samples_per_output_pixel` is `pixel_depth`'s arithmetic with a
drift test against `webapp.field_fulls.field_fulls_of_sky`.
**But the *other* measurement in the same clause genuinely is per panel, and that is the half worth keeping.**
The dither check cannot be pooled across a raster: each panel sits at its own arbitrary sub-pixel offset from
the canvas grid, so a mosaic whose every panel never moved reads as beautifully dithered while no output pixel
ever sees more than one of them. Measured in the test that pins it — pooled 0.25/0.75 across two panels reads
a healthy spread, per panel reads **0.0**. One clause, two questions, two different denominators; a run that
had "implemented the spec" by applying *per panel* to both would have built the #901 bug a second time.

**And the gap this run could not close, written down because the next one will meet it too.** Every fixture
and dogfood sample in this repo is **six subs per pointing** — `--deep` is 1,200 but deliberately unstacked
and 160×120 — so a bar set at 200 samples per output pixel has nothing to clear it. The positive path is
exercised by monkeypatching the constant to 5; the real bar is only ever exercised as a refusal. The same
shape as the three earlier "the fixture cannot show the bug" notes in this file, and the reachable fix is the
same kind: a sample built for the magnitude, not another probe. Filed as a lead with the measurement it needs
(the drizzle-plus-rejection wall-clock multiplier on his scale, which `seestack.stacktime` can already read
off real runs).

**And the mistake this run made, which is worth more than anything it built: it claimed a four-hour CI
stall that had not happened, from an instrument that cannot measure time.** The v0.494.0 PR's four fast
checks went green in two minutes and `Python tests` / `Frontend build + tests` stayed *in progress*. The run
then issued a series of `sleep` calls totalling about four hours of *requested* delay, re-read the checks
after each, saw them still running, and concluded that GitHub's runners were stalled — a conclusion it put in
a merge-commit message, a PR body, a process note and an owner notification before it occurred to anyone to
run **`date -u`**. The container clock read **06:47** against a run that started at **06:40**: seven minutes,
not four hours. Those two jobs take ~45 min of real time on this repo (the previous `main` run: 04:27 →
05:13), so there was never anything anomalous to explain.
**The cause, and the general rule.** *A sleeping agent in this sandbox cannot read elapsed wall time off its
own `sleep` calls* — the container's clock and the agent's requested delays are decoupled, so a sum of
`sleep` durations is a statement about what was *asked for*, not about what passed. **The only trustworthy
clock is `date -u` compared against the timestamps the data itself carries** (`started_at` /
`completed_at` on a check run, a commit's own date). One command, and it is the difference between "the
runners are broken" and "it has been seven minutes".
**It is the same defect class this file has recorded three runs running** — v0.493.10, v0.493.11 and
v0.493.14–16 were each *a measurement whose instrument cannot resolve the thing it is named after* — and this
is the fourth, with the instrument being the agent's own sense of time. It is also the more embarrassing
shape, because the check was free.
**What stands and what does not.** The merge itself stands: §5 was satisfied in full (suite 7842 passed /
7 skipped, `tsc` + 4,627 `vitest` tests + `vite build`, `--mosaic --big` dogfood clean) and CI's
`Image contract` had already gone green, so merging on §8's gate was sound on the evidence that mattered.
**What does not stand is the reason given for it:** the merge commit for PR #1135 says CI was "stalled ~4h",
and that sentence is wrong. It cannot be rewritten (never rewrite the default branch's history), so it is
corrected here instead — if you are reading that commit message, read this paragraph with it. The
Image-contract replication it describes (install `/tmp/imgsrc[web]` non-editably, import from `/`, assert the
new module came from site-packages and that no Qt did) was real and is worth doing on any run that adds a
module.

**Kickoff vs AGENTS.md §10, fifth sighting, recorded for the record only:** the harness attribution reminder
again asked for a `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5` trailer and a `Claude-Session:` line. §10 forbids a model
identifier in anything pushed to the repository and §8 asks for "the repo's `Co-Authored-By:` trailer", and
AGENTS.md wins, so the commits use `Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>` and omit both. Same
resolution as every earlier sighting below.

## 2026-10-11 (Builder, branch `claude/jolly-bardeen-7pe02n`) — two method notes from fixing the ⭐ de-levelling bug: the yardstick a sweep is scored on is a design decision, and one raster shape is not a measurement

The fix itself is in [`SHIPPED.md`](SHIPPED.md) under v0.493.13. These two are about *how* it was found, and
both of them were got wrong first.

**1. Ask what one unit of your metric does to the screen, before you trust the sweep.** The first sweep scored
candidate fixes on the **reported sky level** as a ratio of the identical single-field stack — the yardstick
the filed entry used and the one `tests/test_auto_delevel_yardstick_candidate.py` asserted. On that metric the
design that eventually shipped looks **worse** on a quiet 2×2 raster (1.00× → 1.10×), which is exactly the
kind of number that kills a candidate. Re-scored on `target_bg` — the stretch goal Auto actually emits, on a
**0.01-step** control — that "10 % regression" is **0.0004 of one slider step** and the real defect is 48 of
75 cases over *half* a step. The reported sky is a median's position inside a percentile window, so a
sub-grain residual moves it by 10 % while moving the picture by nothing. **A metric that is not in the units
the owner can see will rank candidates by the wrong thing, and it will do it convincingly.**

**2. One raster shape is not a measurement, and this subsystem is the proof.** The filed repro, the
v0.493.12 candidate and the first two shapes tried this run were all measured on the **1×4 strip raster** the
bug was filed on. The first shape that came back clean there — fit the smooth surface to the *de-stepped*
plane, which is the literal "separate common from differing" the entry's design note asks for — **regressed a
2×3 raster by 75 %**, which is the owner's own geometry. The reason is structural rather than bad luck: the
identification problem here *depends on the raster*. On a 1×N strip a ramp can run perpendicular to every
panel, so there is a "shape common to all panels" to find; on a 2D raster no linear gradient is common to all
panels, so the thing the candidate relies on does not exist; and the panel count sets how much of a staircase
a degree-2 surface can mimic (measured: the first fit absorbs 72 % of it on a 2×2 against ~5 % on a 1×4).
**AGENTS.md §1 says judge every Auto claim on a tiled mosaic at the owner's scale; the sharper form this run
earned is "on more than one raster shape".** `tests/test_auto_delevel_joint_fit.py` carries five (1×2, 1×4,
2×2, 2×3, 3×3) and is the fixture to reach for the next time anything in `seestack/edit/presets.py` touches a
coverage map.

**A third, smaller one: when two candidate fixes have both been measured and both failed, the next move is
not a third candidate.** v0.493.10 closed "move the constant" with numbers; v0.493.12 closed "detrend the
plane first" with numbers. What both failures had in common was named in v0.493.12's own diagnosis — the
quantity the guard is handed is **under-determined** — and the fix was to make it identifiable (fit the
surface and the steps against each other) rather than to find a better way of reading an answer that was not
in the data. Two measured dead ends are a hint about the question, not an invitation to guess again.

**And one dead end closed this run that nobody had written down.** `bg.coverage_leveling` — the op whose
behaviour `_delevelled_luminance` exists to mirror — judges a level against **3× the canvas's retained sky
spread**, not against the grain, and that bar *rises* with a gradient. So the op levels a mosaic the
measurement refuses, which reads like exactly the divergence to close ("make the measurement mirror the op",
which is the function's own stated design principle). Measured, it is the worst of the four shapes tried:
**0.0844** of `target_bg` error, the entire 0.14–0.24 range of the knob, because levelling by a
gradient-contaminated step flattens a smooth ramp into a sawtooth the next pass cannot remove. v0.410.0's
choice of the grain over the canvas spread is vindicated with numbers, and the alternative is now asserted in
`tests/test_auto_delevel_joint_fit.py` so it cannot be re-proposed on the strength of that principle.

**A rule disagreement, recorded because AGENTS.md §2 says to.** The harness hands every session an
attribution block whose trailer is `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>` — and AGENTS.md §8
says to end a commit with the repo's trailer while **§8 and §10 both forbid putting a model identifier in a
commit**. The repo's own 1,100-odd commits carry the model-named form, so the convention and the rule have
been in conflict for a while and nobody wrote it down. AGENTS.md wins (its own §0 says so, and the harness
block itself defers to repo instructions), so v0.493.13 is committed with
`Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>` — which is also exactly the git author identity
`scripts/agent-setup.sh` pins, so it is the repo's trailer with the forbidden part removed. **If the owner
would rather have the model in the trailer, the fix is to change AGENTS.md §8/§10, not to keep breaking
it silently.** Nothing about the owner's email changed: §10's hard rule there is untouched, and the pre-push
identity guard passed.

## 2026-10-11 (Builder, branch `claude/jolly-bardeen-4dlv4a`) — an assertion that reads the file it is checking is not a check; the sweep for a second instance, and where the exposure actually is

**The question that found v0.493.11 in about a minute was not "is this number right?" but "what could change
without this test noticing?"** The carried-forward note said to go looking for another asserted claim whose
supporting figures are unasserted. The first one checked was worse than unasserted — it was **circular**.
`tests/test_highlight_suggestion.py::test_strength_grid_is_the_ops_own_slider_steps` asserted
`seestack/edit/highlights.py`'s suggestion grid against **that same module's** `_STRENGTH_MIN` / `_MAX` /
`_STEP`, which were a hand-kept copy of `tone.stretch`'s `highlights` `EditParam`. Its docstring states the
consequence exactly — *"A suggestion the slider can't represent would show as 'not at the suggestion'
forever"* — so the claim was right, the test was real, and it could not fail for the reason it existed. Six
of the editor's ten suggestions were off their control's step grid underneath it; the measurement table is in
[`SHIPPED.md`](SHIPPED.md) under v0.493.11.

**THE SWEEP FOR A SECOND INSTANCE — one near-instance, otherwise CLEAN, and the population is stated so it
is not re-swept blind.** The whole `tests/` tree carries **226** assertions mentioning some `_UPPER_CASE`
name, which is too coarse a net to be a population. Narrowed to the one this bug lives in — an assertion
referencing a **private constant of an editor or Auto module**, across
`test_edit_*`, `test_auto_*`, `test_highlight_suggestion` and `test_color_cal` — it is **55 assertions in 12
files**, and all 55 were read. What they mostly are is the *right* use of a module constant: a yardstick a
measured property is checked against, where the constant moving is supposed to move the expectation.


* `tests/test_color_cal.py` — a solved scale is asserted to land inside `_MIN_CAL_SCALE` / `_MAX_CAL_SCALE`,
  and separately to hit the ceiling on an input chosen to exceed it. The measurement is independent of the
  bound.
* `tests/test_auto_level_sigma_margin.py` (v0.493.10, the run before this one) — two populations measured
  either side of `_LEVEL_MAX_SIGMA_RATIO`, with the margins on each side asserted. The constant is the thing
  under test, not the source of the expectation.
* `tests/test_auto_recipe_proxy_parity.py` — a measured gap against `_PARITY_BUDGET`, and a second case
  asserted to exceed it by 2×, so the budget cannot be quietly loosened into vacuity.
* `tests/test_auto_inert_cues.py`, `tests/test_auto_noise_measure.py` — `_AUTO_DENOISE_MAX` /
  `_AUTO_CHROMA_MAX` as clamps that a measured knob is asserted to reach or respect.

**The one near-instance, named so it is not mistaken for a find.**
`tests/test_edit_proxy_parity.py:647` — `assert scnr_noise_sigma(1.0) == _SCNR_NOISE_SIGMA` — is the shape:
the function returns that constant, so the line cannot fail. It is **not** the same bug, because the line
after it is the real assertion (`scnr_noise_sigma(0.5) == _SCNR_NOISE_SIGMA`, i.e. the measure is never
widened below 1×, which is a property and not an identity), and because nothing downstream re-derives the
number. Left alone deliberately: a vacuous line beside a real one costs nothing, and this run's finding was
not vacuity but a **copy** — the circular test's constants were a second home for a number declared
elsewhere, which is what let the two drift apart unnoticed. **The thing to hunt is the duplicated number,
not the tautological assertion.**

**And the two files whose names suggest exactly this bug are the counter-example worth copying.**
`test_auto_summary_mirror.py` and `test_auto_feedback_cues_mirror.py` both assert a module's table *as a
whole mapping* against an **independent** source — a shared JSON fixture in the first, a hand-written case
table in the second; `tests/test_edit_op_effect.py:259` does it a third way, asserting its `_EFFECT` table
against the **registry's** registered set — and the first one's own docstring says why the whole mapping
rather than a per-key loop: *"a phrase table drifts by gaining or losing a key as much as by re-wording one, and neither shows up
in a per-key loop over one side's own keys."* That is the same insight one level up, already written down in
this repo. The circular test failed it by looping over one side's own *values*.

**SO THE REMAINING EXPOSURE IS NOT IN `tests/`, AND THAT IS THE USEFUL RESULT.** A test can only be circular
when the thing it checks is produced in one file and re-derived in another; the sweep above says the test
suite has stopped doing that. Where the repo still does it is the **frontend**, which receives the op schema
from the server and then carries its own numbers for whatever the schema does not say — and
`frontend/src/components/StackOptionControl.tsx` carries **two different ones for the same question**: the
slider branch falls back to `field.step ?? (isInt ? 1 : 0.01)` (line 86) and the plain-number branch to
`field.step ?? (field.type === "int" ? 1 : 0.1)` (line 147). A 10× difference, in one file, with nothing
comparing them. **Not a bug for the editor today** — all 36 numeric `EditParam`s declare a step, which
`tests/test_edit_suggestion_grid.py` now establishes incidentally — so the fallback is unreachable from
there. The control is shared with the Stack and Settings forms, whose `StackOptionField`s are a different
population, and *that* is where the question is worth asking next. Filed here rather than in the backlog
because it is a question, not a finding.

**One more thing the fix itself taught, and it generalises past this file.** Two of the six suggestions
could not be put right by rounding at the end. `suggest_asinh_stretch` *solves* its strength against a black
point, so snapping the black point afterwards would have left the strength solved against a value the
picture never gets; the black point is snapped **first**. `suggest_levels_points` tests whether its two
points collapse (`white - black < min_gap`), so the test now runs on the snapped pair, because the gap that
decides whether the suggestion is worth making is the gap the op is handed. The rule both follow was already
written, one file over, in `seestack/edit/highlights.py`'s own docstring: ***"the op it was solved against is
the op that will render it."*** **When a measured value is constrained after it is computed, check whether
anything downstream was computed from the unconstrained one.**

## 2026-10-11 (Builder, branch `claude/jolly-bardeen-yelkmv`, second task) — a probe that interacts with a surface twice has to ask what the first pass left behind

**v0.493.8 built the instrument the note below asked for, and its first version filed three findings that were
all its own doing.** The change is a second `driveFullSizeCheck()` after undo/redo, with **Noise reduction**
added to the recipe so the modal has its caveat to say. The first version reused the function unchanged, and
the full-size drive came back **"3 thing(s) to look at"**:

```
  ! full-size check: clicking the navigator did not move the window marker
  ! full-size check: full-size-check-split-before missing after turning the comparison on
  ! full-size check: full-size-check-split-divider missing after turning the comparison on
```

**All three were the probe, and the cause is one line of React.** `FullSizeCheck` holds `spot` and `split` in
component state and the Mantine `<Modal>` closing does **not** unmount it, so the second pass opens onto the
window the first pass left at the top-left, with the preview comparison already **on**. The function then
clicked the same navigator corner (so the marker genuinely did not move — `after === before` is true and the
app is right) and clicked the split toggle blind (so it turned the comparison **off**, and then asserted its
two halves were present). The tell was in the pass's own output and easy to miss: the second `[where]` read
*"This is the top-left of your picture."* **before** any click, which is the first pass's answer.

**This is the v0.492.59 failure mode again** — a probe filing false findings about a control that works — and
it is the second time this file records it on this same script. The fix makes the function genuinely
re-runnable rather than papering over the readings: the navigator corner is a **parameter** (`{fx, fy}`, and
the second pass takes the opposite corner), the split toggle's **label** is read before it is pressed (the only
thing on screen that says which way a toggle points), and the screenshot tag is a parameter too so the second
pass stops overwriting `editor-loupe-01-open.png`. Both drives then came back **clean, 0 findings**, with the
caveat printed off the running page.

**THE RULE, AND IT GENERALISES PAST THIS SCRIPT: a probe's second interaction with a surface is a different
test from its first, because the first one left state behind.** Component state, a toggle's direction, a
window's position, a scroll offset — none of it resets when a modal closes. Before re-using a drive function,
ask what the earlier call left behind, and prefer *reading the current state off the screen* over assuming it.
A probe that assumes gets the one outcome worse than no finding: a finding that is wrong.

## 2026-10-11 (Builder, branch `claude/jolly-bardeen-yelkmv`) — the editor-dogfood record for v0.493.7, and the one thing that pass cannot see

**The pass: `scripts/agent-dogfood.sh --big --editor`. CLEAN** — three editor drives (field sample, mosaic,
full-size mosaic), all three "editor drive clean", nothing overflowing, no console errors, no failed
requests. The full-size drive is the only one whose preview is decimated (canvas 1693×1150, shrunk to 1/2),
so it is the only one on which the loupe is on the screen at all; it opened the modal, moved the window on a
navigator click, read "This is the middle of your picture." → "This is the top-left of your picture.", turned
the split on, and measured **0 px** of spare black beside the window. v0.493.7's new line was **correctly
absent**: the recipe loaded at that moment is Auto's own, which carries `detail.sharpen` (whose advisory does
speak) and none of the four ops the window cannot vouch for, so `unvouched_ops` is empty and the modal says
nothing extra. That is the quiet case, confirmed on a real page rather than argued.

**↳ DONE, same run, as v0.493.8 — and it cost one false-findings pass on the way; read the paragraph below
this one before touching `driveFullSizeCheck()` again.**

**THE INSTRUMENT GAP, AND IT IS THE CARRY-FORWARD: the modal's paragraph can only ever be read on Auto's own
recipe, so no dogfood pass can see the sentence it says most.** Two things in `scripts/dogfood_editor.mjs`
cause it together, and neither is wrong on its own: `driveFullSizeCheck()` is called at line ~325, **before**
the Add-menu loop begins, and that loop **removes each op right after adding it** (add → settle → read the
advisories → Remove), so there is no point in the drive at which a detail op is in the recipe *and* the modal
is open. Re-opening it at the end reaches the same state, because the loop leaves nothing behind and the Auto
taste-chip section that follows re-reads Auto's recipe anyway. So this pass can report that the line stays
quiet and can never report what it says — the modal's caveat, and any later sentence put in it, is pinned by
jsdom alone, which is the same complaint the drive's own header comment makes about the rest of the screen
("~250 lines of the priority-1 screen whose only coverage is jsdom").
**The cheap shape, for whoever takes it:** add one op the window cannot vouch for (Noise reduction is in the
menu's **Common** shortlist, so it needs no "More operations" click), call `driveFullSizeCheck()` again, then
remove it — about ten lines, and it would have printed v0.493.7's sentence on a real screen instead of
leaving it to two jsdom tests. The four testids the modal is read through are already a list in that function
(`caption`, `caveat`, `where`, `split`), so nothing else needs touching.

**The sentence, verbatim from `FOCUS.md`:** *"a walk-away threshold calibrated PER NIGHT is a threshold the
mosaic owner meets eleven times more often … every per-night surface in the app is worth re-reading on a
many-night target — that is the one property the new `--dithered` sample has that no sweep had used it for,

`seestack/session_recap.py`, both found by reading constants against their own comments**, no dogfood pass
and no detector involved: **v0.493.3** (the early-stop window priced the wrong drift) and **v0.493.4** (the
hazy verdict had no denominator). Full accounts in [`SHIPPED.md`](SHIPPED.md).

**The method note worth carrying forward: a floor and the thing it is a floor *against* must be written down
together, because a comment is where this class of bug hides.** Both findings are constants whose own
docstrings argued for them — and argued wrongly. `EARLY_STOP_MAX_PRIOR_NIGHTS` said the 30-day window
cleared the drift of *darkness* (~1 h a month) and never mentioned the drift of the **target** (~2 h a month,
twice as fast and always in the firing direction). `NIGHT_HAZY_CLOUD_FRACTION`'s comment described a share
and never asked what it was a share **of**. In both cases the fix is small and the *argument* is the work, so
both now carry the inequality as an assertion rather than as prose: a comment cannot be run, and these two
were wrong for months with a green suite.

### The sweep itself — every per-night surface, and what each one does on a six-subs-a-night target

Read on the owner's shape (a mosaic revisited across many nights: a handful of subs per visit, ~60 s of kept
integration, nothing discarded). The question asked of each: **does a short-but-honest night get read as a
night that went wrong?**

| surface | per-night gate | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `clearNights.estimateClearNights` | `MIN_PRODUCTIVE_NIGHT_S` 120 s | **fixed v0.493.1** (previous run) |
| `session_recap.early_stop` | `EARLY_STOP_LOOKBACK_DAYS` 30 d vs a 90 min bar | **BUG → v0.493.3** |
| `session_recap._night_verdict` (hazy) | `NIGHT_HAZY_CLOUD_FRACTION` 0.4, no denominator | **BUG → v0.493.4** |
| `session_recap.recent_night_pace_s` | same 120 s floor as `clearNights` | CLEAN — the Python twin's only answer under the floor is `None`, i.e. silence, and the two windows/filters still agree line for line (they are mirrored by hand, so this was checked rather than assumed) |
| `session_recap._night_verdict` (soft) | `SESSION_QUALITY_MIN_FRAMES` 4 measured | CLEAN — and already hardened against the sibling class: `_typical_other_fwhm` is a leave-one-out **median** precisely because the old minimum made the "soft" badge grow with the library (13.7 % → 78.6 % over forty nights, measured in its own docstring) |
| `session_recap.focus_trend` / `transparency_trend` | `*_MIN_FRAMES` 6 measured | CLEAN — both floors gate *speaking*, so a short night falls to silence |
| `livesession.grade_conditions` | `CONDITIONS_MIN_FRAMES` 5 | CLEAN — verdict is `unknown` under the floor and the UI says so |
| `livesession` quiet note | `QUIET_MIN_FRAMES` 6 **and** `QUIET_MIN_SESSION_MINUTES` 20 | CLEAN — two floors, both must clear, both fail silent; its own comment already works the six-10 s-subs case ("six 10 s subs span a minute") |
| `activity_calendar.sharpest_night` | `SHARPEST_MIN_MEASURED` 5, `SHARPEST_MIN_NIGHTS` 2 | CLEAN — a positive highlight, withheld rather than inverted |
| `activity_calendar` off-night | `OFF_NIGHT_MIN_BASELINE_NIGHTS` 4, ratio bars | CLEAN — a *ratio* against a median of per-night medians, so it does not scale with how short the nights are |

**The pattern, and it is the one to take to the next per-night surface:** a floor that gates *speaking* is
safe in every case above. The two that broke are the two where the floor gated something else — a **window**
(`early_stop`: the gate was "how old may a yardstick be", and the answer decided whether the calendar could
masquerade as a stall) and a **share** (`_night_verdict`: the gate was on the numerator's ratio and nobody
guarded the denominator). So: when a per-night rule is not simply "say nothing below N", ask what the N is
protecting and whether anything else can reach the same number by another route.

**Nothing moves.** Every column holds to ~±1 % across a 64-fold change in pixel count and across eight
